Title: Artificial intelligence anxiety among creative professionals: Evidence from the Brazilian creative economy
Authors: Marco Aurelio de Souza Rodrigues, Veranise Jacubowski Correia Dubeux
Abstract: This study examines the dimensional structure of Artificial Intelligence Anxiety among Brazilian creative professionals through a cross-cultural adaptation and validation of the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS). While the original four-factor structure of the scale—Learning, Job Replacement, AI Configuration, and Sociotechnical Blindness—is broadly replicated, findings from EFA and CFA revealed recurring patterns of greater empirical overlap between factors, lower compartmentalization among anxiety dimensions, and atypical psychometric behavior in specific items when compared to the original validation study. Furthermore, subgroup analyses demonstrate that learning-related anxiety is higher among younger professionals, suggesting that support needs may vary across career stages. These findings are consistent with the proposition that creative workers experience AI anxiety differently from the general-population samples originally used to validate the AIAS. Theoretically, these results extend the AIAS literature to a professional population whose identity is closely tied to authorship and originality, yet whose AI-related anxiety remains empirically understudied. Practically, the findings suggest that managerial responses centered exclusively on technical upskilling may be insufficient to address concerns — such as those tied to human-machine similarity and occupational replacement — that appear to co-occur among creative professionals.

Title: Mapping urban-industrial symbiosis through a business ecosystem lens
Authors: David Tianxin Shang, Yi Sun, Yongjiang Shi
Abstract: This paper examines the evolution of urban industrial symbiosis (UIS) through a business ecosystem lens. UIS, defined as the synergistic integration of urban and industrial systems where waste and by-products are repurposed as industrial inputs, has demonstrated strong potential to address climate change, urbanization challenges, and supply chain vulnerabilities. Existing UIS research has primarily focused on material flows, network structures, and policy arrangements. However, limited attention has been paid to how coordination mechanisms evolve as ecosystem interdependence and complexity increase over time. This omission is consequential because even powerful coordinators face structural limits when coordinating expanding interdependencies among heterogeneous actors and resource flows, creating a coordination gap. Drawing on case studies of Ulsan (South Korea), Händelö (Sweden), EcoPark (Hong Kong), Metro Vancouver (Canada), Kalundborg (Denmark), HS Orka (Iceland), and Kawasaki (Japan), the paper develops a process model of UIS ecosystem coordination that links generation-processing-auxiliary (G-P-A) subsystems, coordination tensions and mechanisms, and governance pathways across three analytical phases. The study advances UIS research by shifting from exchange-oriented perspectives toward dynamic ecosystem coordination and theorizing how coordination mechanisms evolve under increasing ecosystem complexity. It further extends business ecosystem theory by explaining how increasingly distributed coordination capacity sustains ecosystem resilience as growing interdependence strains centralized orchestration.

Title: Using leverage points to identify interventions for transitioning the Dutch road infrastructure sector toward sustainability
Authors: Angie Ruiz, André Nijhof, Maurits Sanders, Fredy Ivar Sierra-Fernández, Joanne Vinke-de Kruijf
Abstract: The transition toward sustainability in infrastructure sectors requires interventions that address systemic lock-ins rather than isolated technological improvements. However, innovation ecosystem research offers only limited guidance on how public-sector-driven ecosystems can be intentionally steered toward sustainability under conditions of structural inertia. This study employs Donella Meadows’ leverage points framework to identify and categorize potential systemic interventions in the Dutch road infrastructure innovation ecosystem. Using an action-oriented research design conducted over 1.5 years with public clients, contractors, and knowledge institutions, the study identifies 25 interventions across five thematic areas. The findings show that interventions predominantly target system design and feedback structures, the strengthening of governance, foresight, and integration capabilities rather than focusing on parameter-level change. This highlights how transformations in public-sector innovation ecosystems emerge through the gradual reconfiguration of rules, information flows, and coordination mechanisms. The study contributes to innovation ecosystem research by demonstrating how leverage points can be used to guide and structure ecosystem-level intervention strategies and support deliberate steering of public-sector-driven innovation ecosystems toward sustainability.

Title: Configuring hybrid agency: How both technological agency and human agency drive blockchain-based risk mitigation
Authors: Yongjun Wei, Steven Si, Yongyi Shou
Abstract: The latest research indicates that blockchain technology (BCT) is a powerful tool for organizational risk management, but enterprises often struggle to fully utilize its potential and effectiveness in practical operations. This study explores the configuration of BCT agency mechanism and human agent mechanism in the idiosyncratic risk mitigation that drives success and failure. By leveraging the hybrid agency theory and employing crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA) on a sample of Chinese listed firms, we identify distinct pathways to risk mitigation success and failure. The findings of this study reveal that successful risk mitigation is not solely dependent on maximizing technical features or application scope; it often depends on strategically limiting the application scope of the technology to match the organization's governance capabilities. On the contrary, failure typically occurs when enterprises over-expand their technology deployment without the necessary internal expertise or platform dominance to manage this expansion. This study challenges technological determinism and emphasizes the necessity of hierarchical control in blockchain governance. Moreover, by shifting the research focus from structured task allocation to configurational coordination of governance capabilities, we have advanced the hybrid agent theory. This indicates that the feasibility of agent technology depends on whether human capabilities are sufficient to coordinate the scope of the deployed technology.

Title: Exploratory versus exploitative innovation in central state-owned enterprises: the role of administrative rank
Authors: Haiping Fu, Hongquan Chen, Saixing Zeng, Ruochen Zeng
Abstract: State-owned enterprises (SOEs) play a pivotal role in national innovation systems, yet their dual mandate of serving public objectives while remaining commercially viable makes it difficult to balance exploratory and exploitative innovation. We examine how administrative rank, a formal position within the party-state hierarchy, shapes this balance in Chinese central SOEs. Using a multi-source panel dataset of Chinese central SOEs from 2003 to 2023 and patent-based measures of exploratory and exploitative innovation, we find that higher administrative rank is primarily associated with greater exploratory innovation, alongside a negative relationship with exploitative innovation. Absorptive capacity reinforces the exploratory orientation associated with administrative rank, whereas deep internal hierarchies attenuate it. These findings suggest that administrative rank shapes innovation portfolios by structuring access to policy-backed resources, frontier knowledge, and strategically salient incentives. By highlighting differentiation within the central SOE sector, this study extends resource-based and incentive-based views of SOE innovation and shows how politically structured organizational position helps explain the allocation of effort between exploration and exploitation.

Title: The designer's turn: Reconfiguring professional identity for project innovation in the generative AI era
Authors: Ming Hung Hsieh, Rong Chen, Hui Chun Lee
Abstract: The disruption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in creative industries is profound. While AI increasingly acts as a proactive partner in ideation, little is known about how this collaboration relates to professional identity reconstruction and project performance. To examine this, we focus on spatial design (architecture and interior design), where digital generation must translate into strict physical constraints and commercial reality. To understand the human foundations of AI-driven innovation, we conducted a mixed-methods study: 10 qualitative interviews (Gioia methodology) and a survey of 223 spatial design projects from Taiwan and Mainland China. Findings support a mediating role for Professional Identity Reconstruction (PIR) between perceived human-AI collaboration and perceived project performance. Specifically, we uncover a shift from the identity of traditional “craftsmen” to “strategic decision-makers.” Professionals who successfully navigate this reconstruction no longer act as mere manual executors; instead, they exercise strategic judgment over machine-generated outputs. This strategic elevation is associated with an enhanced ability to interpret, constrain, and translate raw AI variations into valuable project outcomes. This paper offers two key contributions. First, it refines the assumption of automatic technological dividends: while direct human-AI collaboration correlates with internal process efficiency, it has an indirect association with external market success through human strategic translation. Second, it advances innovation management literature by conceptualizing PIR as one plausible translating pathway. Our findings suggest that as AI automates execution, the realization of market value shifts toward strategic direction. Ultimately, we advise managers to foster workflows prioritizing human evaluative inputs, ensuring algorithmic capabilities are firmly anchored within professional boundaries and commercial realities.

Title: Resource orchestration in incubator management: Evidence from multiple cases
Authors: Xuelin Wang, Xiaofeng Qin, Yeming Gong, Ajay Kumar, Xinyuan Lu
Abstract: Incubators play a vital role in entrepreneurial ecosystems by providing start-ups with resources such as funding, mentorship, and access to networks. Incubator systems differ from traditional organizations because start-ups remain legally and strategically independent, which limits hierarchical control and makes coordination inherently relational. However, existing research tends to emphasize the effects of individual resources, paying less attention to how incubators orchestrate resources through ongoing interaction with ventures, leaving unresolved why incubators with similar resource bases often produce markedly different outcomes. Thus, drawing on Resource Orchestration Theory, this study examines how incubators structure, bundle, and leverage resources, and how orchestration operates across multiple levels to shape start-up growth and incubator performance. Based on a qualitative multi-case study, we identify a four-stage cyclical orchestration process in which incubators (1) structure a foundational resource base, (2) provide tailored initial resource packages, (3) dynamically reconfigure bundled resources as ventures evolve, and (4) activate start-up feedback. Feedback takes concrete forms such as alumni mentoring, network bridging, investment connections, and reputational endorsements, which replenish the incubator's resource base and enable subsequent rounds of support. We further theorize a multi-level mechanism comprising incubator orchestration, start-up orchestration, and joint orchestration; joint orchestration operates through coordinated resource acquisition, bundling, and leveraging, helping explain outcome heterogeneity beyond resource stock differences.

Title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee innovation: Collaboration modes, idea journey, and decline in creative psychological ownership
Authors: Ling Tan, Xin Cao, Chunlan Ou, Ya Li, Xiaojie Wu
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used by employees to support creative idea generation, yet less is known about its psychological consequences for employees’ subsequent willingness to remain engaged with those ideas. Drawing on psychological ownership theory, we examine whether GAI usage is associated with lower creative psychological ownership (CPO)—the extent to which employees perceive creative ideas as “theirs”—and, in turn, weaker intentions to elaborate, champion, and implement those ideas. We further propose that this relationship varies across human–GAI collaboration modes, with the negative relationship between GAI usage and CPO being more pronounced under GAI-centric collaboration than under human-centric or symbiotic collaboration. Across two scenario-based experiments (Studies 1–2), two task-based studies involving actual GAI interaction (Studies 3–4), and a multi-wave field study (Study 5), the findings provide converging, although not uniform, evidence for the proposed relationships. A mini meta-analysis further indicates an overall negative association between GAI usage and CPO and positive associations between CPO and downstream innovation-related intentions. Overall, the findings identify a potential psychological cost of GAI-assisted idea generation. They also show how collaboration modes may shape employees’ perceived ownership of ideas and their intentions to continue developing and advancing them.

Title: How does digital transformation and Global Innovation Network Embedding affect ESG performance of multinational enterprises? Empirical evidence from an Eastern innovation pattern
Authors: Jintao Lu, Zuxin Song, Luu Duc Toan Huynh, Malin Song, Armando Papa
Abstract: As an important manifestation of data-driven technological innovation paradigms, digital transformation has become a key pathway through which multinational enterprises reshape their innovation processes, enhance global competitiveness, and achieve sustainable value creation. It not only transforms firms’ modes of knowledge creation, organizational coordination mechanisms, and resource allocation logic, but also creates new opportunities for multinational enterprises to deepen their global innovation network embedding and improve ESG performance. However, existing studies have rarely systematically explored the impact mechanism of digital transformation on ESG performance from the perspective of global innovation network embedding. Grounded in the resource-based theory and social network theory, using panel data of Chinese A-share listed multinational enterprises from 2010 to 2022, the impact and mechanism of digital transformation on ESG performance in multinational enterprises were empirically analyzed by employing the two-way fixed effects model, the mediation effect model and the moderation effect model. Results indicate that, (1) Digital transformation has a significantly positive effect on the ESG performance. (2) The mechanism through which digital transformation enhances ESG performance lies in accelerating the global innovation network embedding of multinational enterprises. (3) Internal control quality strengthens the positive effect of digital transformation on ESG performance, whereas external environmental uncertainty weakens this effect. (4) The digital transformation has a stronger incentive effect on ESG performance for large-scale, manufacturing, and technology and labor-intensive multinational enterprises. The obtained conclusions contribute to fully leveraging the driving effect of digital transformation by multinational enterprises in the global value chain and provide empirical evidence that such firms can enhance their global collaborative innovation capability and sustainable competitive advantage through digital transformation.

Title: PATTERN-X: Guiding sustainable innovation in intelligent lighting systems through an explainable AI framework for technology convergence forecasting
Abstract: Strategic R&D management requires foresight tools that are dynamic, uncertainty-aware, and transparent, yet most existing approaches remain static, deterministic, and difficult to interpret. This study introduces PATTERN-X (Patent Analytics Through Temporal Network Evaluation and Reasoning with eXplainability), an explainable AI framework integrating temporal patent network analysis, Bayesian deep learning, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Using 4167 European Patent Office patents in the Intelligent Lighting Systems (ILS) domain (1981–2024), the framework is empirically validated within the European ILS innovation ecosystem. The study addresses three research questions: RQ1 examines how temporal network analysis can reveal the evolution of technology innovation ecosystems; RQ2 investigates how probabilistic deep learning can quantify predictive uncertainty for risk-aware R&D decision-making; and RQ3 explores how generative AI can translate quantitative forecasts into evidence-based strategic narratives. Addressing RQ1, temporal co-classification network analysis reveals ecosystem evolution from 3 to 16 technology clusters and a shift in centrality toward digital control and vehicle-integrated technologies. Addressing RQ2, a Bayesian LSTM achieves an MAE of 0.89, an 88% strategic hit rate, and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates (PICP = 0.91 against a nominal 95% interval, reflecting a slight undercoverage typical of variational approximations), enabling risk-sensitive evaluation of convergence opportunities. Addressing RQ3, a CPC-guided RAG system generates evidence-grounded strategic narratives with high faithfulness (0.85; κ = 0.82), translating probabilistic forecasts into auditable managerial explanations. Together, these results demonstrate how dynamic analysis, uncertainty quantification, and explainable generative AI can enhance technology convergence forecasting and strategic innovation management.

Title: Institutionalizing portfolio entrepreneurship: the Venture Studio model
Authors: Davide Viglialoro, Giuliano Sansone, Elisa Ughetto, Paolo Landoni, Martin Lukeš
Abstract: Venture Studios (VSs) are organizations that create start-ups by acting as founders or co-founders and operating through standardized venture creation processes conducted in parallel. To examine this organizational model and delineate its distinctiveness from others, we developed a global database, conducted multiple case studies with twelve European VSs and two international networks, and administered a worldwide survey. Drawing on human capital and organizational learning perspectives, this study identifies the architectural characteristics and mechanisms through which VSs institutionalize portfolio entrepreneurship. Our findings reveal how VSs convert individual entrepreneurial expertise into organizationally codified human capital. In doing so, VSs extend entrepreneurial agency and cognition from individuals to organizations, offering an organizational model for parallel venture creation. Finally, we clarify how VSs complement other entrepreneurial actors by reducing early-stage uncertainty and generating validated, investment-ready ventures.

Title: From creative output to creative governance: Legitimizing AI-generated creativity under deepfake uncertainty
Authors: Domitilla Magni, Giuseppe Lanfranchi, Maria Esmeralda Palaganas
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges established foundations of innovation legitimacy by decoupling output quality from human effort, intention, and responsibility. When creative outputs no longer provide reliable signals of human agency, legitimacy judgments must be reconstructed through alternative interpretive cues. This study reconceptualizes innovation legitimacy as an inferential process formed under conditions of technological opacity and examines how governance practices shape legitimacy judgments in AI-mediated creativity. Drawing on a survey-based experiment (N = 240), we investigate how configurations of AI involvement, transparency timing, and deepfake-related manipulation cues influence perceived deception, perceived human effort, and perceived authenticity. Legitimacy judgments, operationalized as inferential assessments of deception, effort, and authenticity, are distinguished from their downstream attitudinal and behavioral consequences. The findings show that legitimacy in AI-mediated creativity shifts from output-based evaluation toward governance-dependent sensemaking. Transparency operates as an interpretive mechanism whose effects depend critically on timing, while deepfake cues systematically heighten moral uncertainty and undermine legitimacy. By specifying the microfoundations through which legitimacy breaks down and is partially reconstructed under AI-induced opacity, the study advances innovation theory by reframing legitimacy as a governance-dependent inferential achievement. This reframing differs from existing interpretive and institutional accounts: governance is conceptualized not as a mechanism that generates legitimacy directly through compliance or ceremonial conformity, but as an interpretive infrastructure that shapes the conditions under which audiences can form legitimacy judgments when conventional output-based cues are absent. The findings contribute to debates on AI governance, innovation diffusion, and responsible innovation in contexts characterized by ambiguous agency and uncertainty about algorithmic production processes.

Title: Frugal business models: A systemic perspective from the international literature
Authors: Ana Paula Provin, Ademar Dutra, José Baltazar S.O. A. Guerra, Ana Regina de Aguiar Dutra, Anelise Leal Vieira Cubas
Abstract: Frugal business models have emerged as innovative alternatives for serving low-income markets through affordable, sustainable, and robust solutions, supporting organizational strategies under conditions of resource constraints. Initially developed in the context of emerging economies, these models have increasingly gained relevance in developed countries as well, driven by growing concerns regarding resource efficiency and sustainable consumption. Despite the rising academic interest in frugal innovation, research on frugal business models remains fragmented, with limited consolidation of their defining characteristics, dominant patterns, and broader impacts. To address this gap, this study conducts a systematic literature review using the ProKnow-C method. The analysis of a final portfolio of 74 articles identified 23 illustrative cases of frugal products and services and enabled the mapping of recurring patterns, strategic logics, and challenges associated with frugal business models. The findings indicate that these models can support sustainable innovation strategies; however, further empirical research is required to assess their impacts across both emerging and developed market contexts. Overall, this study contributes to the literature by synthesizing existing knowledge and outlining avenues for future research in this domain.

Title: Editorial Board
A review on blockchain-driven e-healthcare service user empowerment
Authors: Anjali Shishodia, Rohit Sharma, Angappa Gunasekaran, Prikshat Verma
Abstract: This paper aims to conduct a hybrid study focusing on blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment and its applications in e-healthcare concepts, using bibliometric, network, thematic, and content analyses. The study considered 778 published articles from 2016 to 2024 and conducted a network analysis of the 49 most-cited articles in the domain of blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment. The results underscore the underlying research areas, which are further clustered into five major principles, namely, data ownership and control, data privacy and security, trust and transparency, incentivization and engagement, and accessibility and equity. The results offer unique insights for theoretical and managerial implications and propose a conceptual framework for future study in this sector.

Title: How sharing-platform SMEs innovate their business models in developing economies: A process and ecosystem perspective
Authors: Sara Odat, Omar Al-Tabbaa, Zaheer Khan, George Saridakis
Abstract: Sharing-platform small and medium-sized enterprises (SPSMEs) are a critical player in the sharing economy. However, how they innovate their business models in the developing economies setting is still unclear. This is because most research focuses on large sharing-platform firms in developed economies, often treating their business models as relatively static configurations, while explaining their innovation mainly from the firm's internal perspective. Accordingly, we ask: how SPSMEs, that operate in developing economies, adapt and reconfigure their business models over time while responding to challenging external conditions (including weak institutions, regulatory uncertainty, low digital awareness, fragmented provider networks, and limited ecosystem support). Drawing on multiple-case studies comprising seven SPSMEs in Jordan and the UAE, we develop a 3Ts process model (Triggering, Theming and Transforming) which explains how SPSMEs recognise opportunities, define value logics, and reconfigure their digital activity systems over time. We also show that the SPSMEs business ecosystem consists of two networks (the Digital Activity Network and the Digital Business Network), whose actors enable, constrain and redirect the business model innovation process. The study contributes to research on business model innovation (BMI) and the sharing economy literature by showing that BMI in SPSMEs is not a one-off design outcome. Rather, it is an evolving and context-sensitive process shaped by firm-level adaptation and business ecosystem conditions, particularly in developing economies.

Title: Causes of crowdsourcing in science failures: a multi-level approach
Authors: Regina Lenart, Marta Najda-Janoszka, Jin Chen
Abstract: Crowdsourcing in science is an increasingly popular complementary method of conducting scientific research. However, organizing a crowdsourcing in science initiative is a challenge for scientists, and many such initiatives fail. Nevertheless, the literature on failures of crowdsourcing in science and their causes is still in its infancy, and the results to date are scattered and fragmented. Drawing on a multilevel perspective, we recognize, characterize and offer a structured understanding of the causes of the failure of crowdsourcing in science. We collected data using focus group interviews with 36 scholars representing various scientific fields and disciplines. The results show that the causes of failure are the initiator's insufficient competences, their negative attitude towards crowdsourcing in science, insufficient organisational support, the compulsory nature of crowdsourcing in science, and the crisis of trust in science. In addition, normative pressure and technology connect the interactions within and between levels. On the basis of these findings, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that structures the causes of the failure of crowdsourcing in science, and takes into account interactions within and between levels. The results and the framework serve as the basis for offering implications for researchers, managerial staff of institutions of higher education and decision-makers. We show how important crowdsourcing in science is, and that careful management of such projects is workable.

Title: What makes an effective ideator? The distinct roles of cognition, personality, and experience in early-stage venture ideation
Authors: Thomas Maran, Anna Bachmann, Sascha Kraus, Tobias Fitz, Marco Furtner, Marina Dabić
Abstract: A microfoundational account of organizational innovation capability should explain which individual-level attributes distinguish ideators who are better able to generate, select, and elaborate ideas into investment-worthy business concepts. Yet research remains fragmented because prior studies often examine isolated traits and fail to distinguish among key creative ideation outcomes. Drawing on Trait Activation Theory, we conceptualize venture ideation as a staged, trait-relevant context in which cognitive abilities, personality traits, and creative domain experience are differentially expressed across successive stages. We examine this theorizing using a task-based assessment that separates idea quantity , idea originality , and idea quality . Innovation-exposed experts, including R&D experts, managers, and entrepreneurs (n = 208), generated multiple business ideas for a disruptive technology, selected their most promising idea, and refined it into a product or service concept incorporating core elements of a viable business model. Experienced technology-focused venture capitalists evaluated idea quality by indicating whether these concepts merited investment interest. We quantified semantic distinctiveness using multiple large language models as a semantic proxy for selected-idea originality. Divergent thinking predicted idea quantity, but not investor-evaluated idea quality. In contrast, investment-interest judgments were predicted by ideators’ Openness to Experience, creative domain experience, and convergent thinking ability. Overall, our findings show that early-stage venture ideation is not a unitary creative process. Different attributes help ideators generate many ideas and develop selected ideas into investment-worthy business model concepts, advancing a microfoundational account of organizational innovation capability in technology-based venture creation.

Title: Technological relatedness in green innovation disruptiveness: the role of entry pace and rhythm
Authors: Shijun Mu, Lutao Ning, Jin Chen
Abstract: Achieving disruptive innovation in new green technology domains (NGTDs) is essential for firms seeking sustainable competitive advantage, addressing climate challenges, and complying with increasingly stringent regulations. Building on research on technological relatedness and entry strategies, this study argues that although entering NGTDs enables firms to pursue technological leadership, the disruptiveness of their subsequent green innovations may be constrained by the technological relatedness between their existing knowledge bases and the new green domains. Moreover, this negative effect is shaped by firms’ NGTD entry patterns. Using patent data from 994 Chinese listed firms from 2008 to 2016 and applying a Heckman selection model, we find that technological relatedness reduces the disruptiveness of green innovation. An irregular entry rhythm exacerbates this negative effect, whereas a faster entry pace mitigates it. These findings advance the literature by integrating the concepts of pace and rhythm of entry into studies of green innovation and by providing evidence from an emerging economy context. The results suggest that firms should balance reliance on existing technological trajectories with exploration of new knowledge bases to enhance disruptive outcomes. This study offers actionable insights for firms and policymakers seeking to accelerate green technological transitions and foster more disruptive, high-impact environmental innovation.

Title: Government support, co-creation, and digital transformation on the road to sustainable innovation
Authors: Ana Colovic, Annalisa Caloffi, Alan Bandeira Pinheiro
Abstract: This study examines whether and how different types of government support (financial, technological, market) impact the three types of co-creation efforts (product, process, and knowledge co-creation) of SMEs and how these, in turn, impact sustainable innovation outcomes. It also investigates whether digital transformation mediates the positive relationship between the three types of co-creation and sustainable innovation. The conceptual model is tested on an original dataset of 188 SMEs in France, collected in 2025. Findings indicate that product co-creation is positively affected by government technological support, and knowledge co-creation by market support. The mediation effect of digital transformation is confirmed for the relationship between product co-creation and sustainable innovation, while process and knowledge co-creation directly lead to sustainable innovation. The implications of the study for research, policy and practice are discussed.

Title: Digital platform archetypes as catalysts for circular economy innovation in technology industries
Abstract: Digital platform technologies are reshaping traditional linear value chains and are increasingly positioned as primary facilitators of circular economy implementation in electronics manufacturing. This study investigates how leading manufacturers, including Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi, and Dell, use digital platforms to support circular strategies through a comparative multi-case analysis of electronics platform archetypes. The analysis identifies two distinct digital platform archetypes. Premium integrated ecosystems, represented by Apple and Samsung, target higher-value consumer segments and emphasise component integration, lifecycle control, and tightly governed proprietary platforms. These models prioritise repair, refurbishment, and lifecycle extension within highly integrated product–service systems. In contrast, accessible ecosystem orchestrators, such as Xiaomi and Dell, promote broader participation across partners and users, focusing on asset management, service modularity, and affordability for price-sensitive consumers and business clients. The findings highlight how platform design influences circular outcomes, with governance structures, business models, and digital infrastructure needing alignment with market positioning and user needs. Overall, the paper contributes to research on digital platforms and circular business models by clarifying how platform archetypes shape pathways toward more circular electronics systems.

Title: Coopetitive portfolio configurations for product innovation: A crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis
Authors: Nina Telg, Paul Chiambaretto, Anne-Sophie Fernandez, Boris Lokshin
Abstract: Firms create and manage coopetitive portfolios (i.e., alliance portfolios including competitors) to foster product innovation, as they provide access to various complementary but also compatible resources and knowledge that are essential for innovation. The presence of competitors in coopetitive portfolios can create specific synergies but also conflicts with other partners that could enhance or limit the occurrence of product innovation. To understand under which combinations of partner types in a coopetitive portfolio product innovation can occur, we use a crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA) on a sample of 921 Dutch firms in the period 2010-2016. We show that alliances with competitors are complementary with customer alliances in promoting the occurrence of product innovation. In addition, our analysis reveals that when ties with universities are present in a coopetitive portfolio, suppliers must be present as well to introduce new products. Finally, we highlight that coopetitive portfolio configurations leading to product innovation vary according to the focal firm's size and industry dynamics.

Title: Teaching to learn and learning to teach: using machine training to develop artificial intelligence partners in new product development
Authors: Andrea Lipparini, Maurizio Sobrero, Korinzia Toniolo
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping how innovation is developed, and new product development (NPD) is an important domain at the centre of this shift, given its data-rich, high-uncertainty contexts. In this paper, we focus on the design and training of AI systems in which human expertise is encoded into machine models and the future scope of human and machine agency is determined. Drawing on organizational learning theory, we argue that training strategies defining who provides labels, which data are used, and how feedback is generated and reused, constitute design decisions that differ in how feedback is recursively structured, where knowledge is located, and how deeply expert judgment is codified. We develop and test three strategies, experiential, nudging, and generative, and instantiate them through computational simulations in the domain of geotechnical services for underwater exploration. We further assess the cross-context portability of the most effective strategy by redeploying the trained model in a second NPD setting. Our results show that strategies that recursively incorporate expert feedback across training cycles produce reliable, transferable models, whereas those that decouple human expertise from the training process converge prematurely on narrow solution spaces. These findings suggest that how firms structure the training of AI systems directly shapes model reliability and transferability, and provide a basis for theorizing how organizational routines, competencies, and relational forms of AI agency may develop as AI systems become embedded in NPD processes.

Title: When innovation fails: Nonlinear effects of innovation failure on trade credit and the moderating role of innovation disclosure
Authors: Lulu Lin, Huaqi Chai, Pengcheng Chen, Xiaodong Geng
Abstract: Trade credit plays a critical role in alleviating firms' short-term financing constraints, yet little is known about how firms adjust their use of trade credit in response to innovation failure. Drawing on the substitution hypothesis between bank credit and trade credit, this study examines how innovation failure, as a firm-level adverse shock, affects firms’ trade credit usage. Using panel data from 296 listed biopharmaceutical firms in China over the period 2007 – 2024, we document a significant U-shaped relationship between innovation failure and trade credit. Specifically, firms’ reliance on trade credit decreases as innovation failure rises from low to moderate levels, reaches its lowest point at moderate levels, and then increases as innovation failure becomes high. We further show that this U-shaped relationship is driven by a substitution mechanism between bank credit and trade credit. In addition, innovation disclosure strengthens the U-shaped relationship by improving information transparency and reducing uncertainty surrounding innovation outcomes. Overall, this study highlights the pivotal role of trade credit in alleviating short-term financing constraints arising from innovation failure from a supply chain finance perspective. It provides new empirical evidence and policy implications for optimizing corporate financing structures through effective supply chain relationship management.

Title: Navigating codified, tacit and novel rules: Mapping the human-AI creativity frontier
Abstract: This paper examines the boundary between human and machine creativity by analysing 593 tasks across 126 occupations in the cultural and creative industries. Theoretically, we propose an evolutionary conceptualisation of creativity, structured around three rule types corresponding to retention (codified), adoption (tacit), and origination (novel) phases. Empirically, using GPT-4, we generate synthetic annotations of the semantic content of task descriptions in the Australian Skills Classification. We derive indicators of cognitive and behavioural rules within tasks and their carriers (human, AI, or hybrid human-AI) to capture creativity, and indicators of AI autonomy feasibility and efficiency potential to capture GenAI exposure scenarios. The agent-rule matching suggests a specialisation of agents in carrying defined, tacit, or novel rules, as well as two mechanisms. The first is the structured novelty effect, whereby AI autonomy feasibility is higher when defined cognitive rules combine with novel rule creation. The second is the tacit knowledge boundary, whereby tacit rules are negatively associated with AI autonomy feasibility. In our interpretation, these mechanisms reflect an efficacy logic (matching the right agent to each rule type) that differs from an efficiency logic (optimising technically feasible gain potentials). Combining both logics, we derive a simulated classification of tasks into three categories. The mixed category, involving hybrid carrier configurations, predominates (86.3%), alongside limited replacement (2.7%) and AI immune (11.0%) categories. We identify two levels of human-AI complementarity. The first lies in rule types within tasks and engages different forms of creativity (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational). The second concerns efficiency potential when performing tasks.

Title: Brokerage, power and individual innovation: When do brokers act on their structural advantage?
Authors: Martha Topete, Nathan Betancourt, Flore Bridoux, Zuzana Sasovova
Abstract: Prior research has found that brokers, those who stand between two disconnected parties, may access non-redundant information that is conducive to higher innovation. However, research has also shown that occupying brokering network positions does not systematically translate into higher innovation; in other words, brokers do not always exploit such structural opportunity. To better understand the conditions under which brokers innovate, we adopt a contingency approach and theorize that the relationship between brokerage and individual innovation is contingent on individuals’ perception of their power over alters, an important aspect of individuals’ representation of the situation they are in. Using a social network analysis at a consulting and training organization in The Netherlands, we found support for our theory: employees perceiving higher power over alters achieved higher innovation in brokering network positions than employees in these positions who perceived lower power over alters.

Title: Unpacking how integrator state-owned enterprises respond to institutional demand tensions in complex product systems innovation
Authors: Guangpei Chen, Jiang Wei, Jiaming Yang
Abstract: As hybrid organizations situated at the nexus of market and state logics, integrator state-owned enterprises (SOEs) face the daunting challenge of navigating competing institutional demands. In the process of CoPS innovation, such tensions coalesce into a persistent trade-off between legitimacy and autonomy. Drawing on an inductive multiple-case study of three large integrator SOEs operating in two representative CoPS domains in China, this study examines how these firms respond to legitimacy–autonomy tensions across different phases of CoPS innovation. We identify two response strategies, namely, aggregate projection and parallel coordination , that address goal conflicts in the goal-setting phase and means conflicts in the resource-allocation phase, respectively. Moreover, we propose a theoretical model illustrating how these mutually constitutive response strategies jointly enable integrator SOEs to secure legitimacy while preserving autonomy in achieving CoPS innovation. These findings deepen the scholars’ understanding of organizational responses to institutional demands, while also contributing to literature on CoPS innovation.

Title: The innovators scalpel: A knowledge-based view of corporate divestitures & technological performance
Abstract: Knowledge is a fundamental strategic resource. While extensive research examines how firms expand their knowledge base through acquisitions, less attention has been given to how firms reshape and optimize their knowledge base through divestitures. Drawing on the Knowledge-Based View (KBV), we conceptualize divestitures as a mechanism for knowledge reconfiguration, akin to an innovator’s scalpel, which firms can use to refine their knowledge stock and enhance their capacity for technological recombination. We argue that, on average, divestitures will weaken a firm’s technological performance because they reduce the size of the firm’s knowledge base, disrupt innovation routines, and create organizational uncertainty. However, we propose that when firms divest in a way that enhances their technological, structural, and organizational focus, we argue divestitures can lead to superior technological performance. We test our hypotheses using a sample of 7,138 firm-year observations, covering 919 unique firms, in 4 high-tech industries, that announced 1,794 divestitures and filed 414,128 patent applications over a 15-year period. Our findings confirm that while divestitures generally disrupt innovation, divestitures that create focus leads to more and higher-quality innovation. In doing so, our study provides theoretical and managerial insights into how firms can use divestitures to shape their knowledge base, to sustain long-term technological competitiveness, and drive innovation performance. Importantly, our study also advances the corporate strategy and innovation literature by demonstrating that divestitures can be used as an innovation scalpel, cutting away the excess, to strengthen knowledge cohesion, flow and governance.

Title: The impact of balance in the policy mix on firm innovation performance: A motivation–opportunity–ability perspective
Authors: Jingjing Guo, Shasha Zhou, Xinyi Ke, Victor Cui
Abstract: Combining technology-push and demand-pull instruments into a policy mix has been widely employed by policymakers to stimulate innovation. Prior empirical studies have primarily investigated the impacts of the balance between the two types of instruments within a policy mix on innovation performance at the macro or meso level, with limited attention given to the roles of micro-level policy recipients and the contexts in which policies are implemented. By integrating the motivation-opportunity-ability framework with the resource-based view and institutional theory, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of how the effectiveness of a balanced policy mix in stimulating innovation is contingent upon the internal and external contexts of policy-recipient firms. Our empirical analyses are based on a panel dataset of 77 listed firms in the solar photovoltaic industry of China from 2012 to 2022. We find that the balance between technology-push and demand-pull policy instruments within a policy mix has a positive effect on firm innovation performance. Moreover, this relationship is contingent upon firms’ internal absorptive capacity and regional institutional development, and their relative importance differs between state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and non-state-owned enterprises (non-SOEs). The moderating effect of absorptive capacity is particularly pronounced for non-SOEs, whereas the moderating effect of regional institutional development is primarily salient for SOEs. This study extends the innovation literature on policy mix by shedding light on the innovation effect of policy mix balance at the micro level and its contingencies.

Title: From value creation to value appropriation: How firms exploit disruptive innovation opportunities in emerging economies
Authors: Feng Zhang, Yajing Fan, Jingjing Wang, Lei Zhu
Abstract: Although emerging economies encourage firms to create value through disruptive innovations, less is known about how firms appropriate value from these innovations. Drawing on the profit from innovation (PFI) framework, this study examines how product disruptiveness influences opportunity exploitation and how this relationship is conditioned by appropriability mechanisms and institutional forces. Based on a multi-wave, multi-informant field survey and a scenario-based experiment, we find that product disruptiveness enhances opportunity exploitation by increasing perceived differentiation and perceived attractiveness. This relationship is reinforced by informal appropriability mechanisms and political ties, but diminished by formal appropriability mechanisms and government support. These findings shift attention from value creation to value appropriation in disruptive innovation research and extend the PFI framework by showing that value appropriation from disruptive innovations depends on the fit between appropriability mechanisms, institutional forces, and disruptive innovation trajectories in emerging economies.

Title: A global analysis of female innovative entrepreneurship and the role of financial development
Authors: Cecilia Alvarez-Vargas, Joan-Lluís Capelleras, Francis J. Greene, Victor Martin-Sanchez
Abstract: Drawing on feminist and institutional perspectives, this study analyses whether women are equally likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship and whether the maturity of debt and equity markets strengthens women's participation. We use data from 71,888 early-stage ventures across 101 countries and show that women are as likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship, once crucial individual and country-level factors are controlled for. Further, we demonstrate that both debt and equity market development positively moderate this relationship. These findings reveal that gender gaps in innovative entrepreneurship reflect structural and institutional conditions rather than intrinsic propensities and highlight the role that financial development plays in supporting female innovative entrepreneurship.

Title: The low-value trap: Sustaining multi-actor collaboration across problem spaces in emerging technology commercialization
Authors: Ferran Giones, Daniel Laufs, Carsten Schultz
Abstract: Despite the potential applications of bio-marine technologies, many promising innovations remain confined to the laboratory, missing potential high-value applications and damaging the overall perception of the emerging technology. Prior research has highlighted the positive impact of multi-actor collaborations on technology development, particularly to bridge the gap between the lab and the market. However, we know little about the mechanisms that sustain productive multi-actor collaboration in emerging technology commercialization and why they prove insufficient as actors move from low-to high-value applications. We study the case of an emerging technology – the utilization and application of fucoidan, a bio-marine extract – to explore how collaboration is sustained among actors as they face the increasing complexity of the technology commercialization for high-value applications. By building on patents and publications and analyzing in-depth interviews, we identify three key mechanisms that support effective collaboration: anchoring a shared vision, coordinating across knowledge boundaries, and structuring an operational framework. We show how these mechanisms need to be recalibrated, not simply scaled, when actors transition across problem spaces from low to high-value applications, and why the failure to do so produces a low-value trap for the emerging technology.

Title: Do industrial robots improve firm productivity in China? The role of management practices
Abstract: Whether industrial robot adoption improves firm productivity remains an open question, with mixed evidence echoing the broader productivity paradox associated with information and communication technologies. This paper examines whether firm-level management quality can help resolve this ambiguity. Using novel firm-level data from the China Employer–Employee Survey, which uniquely combines direct measures of robot capital and management practices, we show that robot adoption is associated with significantly higher total factor productivity. This finding is robust to alternative measures of robot use and productivity, as well as to instrumental variable strategies exploiting exogenous robot-policy shocks and firm-level robot exposure. A difference-in-differences design further supports a causal interpretation. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that these productivity gains are strongly moderated by management quality. In particular, monitoring, target-setting, and managerial incentive practices act as key complements, whereas non-manager incentives do not play a significant moderating role. Further analysis shows that the gap in productivity gains from robot adoption between small and large firms narrows at higher levels of management quality, suggesting that managerial capability is a key constraint on small firms’ returns to industrial robots. These findings help reconcile the mixed evidence on robot productivity and underscore the importance of management improvement programs as a complement to automation policy.

Title: From circularity to sustainability: Leveraging Industry 4.0 for circular and supply chain resilience
Authors: Muhammad Sadiq, Qasim Ali Nisar, Pradeep Kautish, P.R.S. Sarma, Shahbaz Haider
Abstract: Ongoing environmental issues are increasingly challenging the manufacturing sector because of its environmental footprint. These issues, including carbon emissions, intensive resource consumption, large-scale waste generation, and environmental pollution, have stimulated demand for environmentally responsible supply chain practices. The implementation of these practices can be realized through the application of advanced technology, such as Industry 4.0. This study examines the role of Industry 4.0 technologies towards sustainable supply chain performance and investigates the mediating role played by circular supply chain practices and visibility. Moreover, the moderating role of strategic alliances and resilient supply chains was also analyzed. Data were collected using time-lagged research from senior managers working in manufacturing companies in China. PLS-SEM was used to analyse 371 questionnaires. The findings suggest that Industry 4.0 enhances supply chain visibility and circular supply chain practices and improves sustainable supply chain performance. Further, results also show that supply chain resilience moderates the association between circular supply chain practices, supply chain visibility, and sustainable supply chain performance. However, the moderating role of strategic alliances was found to be insignificant. These findings reveal that manufacturing organizations can achieve sustainable supply chain performance by integrating Industry 4.0 into their operations. These findings contribute significantly to Industry 4.0 and the circular economy in academic, managerial, and policy debates, resulting in sustainable supply chains. Potentially, the findings serve to drive sustainable supply chains in developing countries to better manage the digital transition of the manufacturing industry.

Title: Editorial Board
Go your own way: Managerial engagement with regional innovation ecosystems for Industry 4.0 transformation in Belgian SMEs
Authors: Anastassiya Zabudkina, Olivier Lisein, François Pichault
Abstract: While Industry 4.0 (I4.0) has led to the proliferation of policy-driven innovation ecosystems aimed at supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in their digital transformation, limited attention has been paid to how managers engage with these environments in practice. This study examines how SMEs’ managers interpret, evaluate, and mobilise external support within I4.0 Regional Innovation Ecosystems (I4.0 RIE). Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with managers of industrial SMEs in Belgium, we adopt a sense-making perspective to analyse engagement as an interpretive process. The findings show that managers approach these ecosystems as overlapping support mechanisms, which they evaluate in terms of accessibility and usability and enact through selective, adaptive, and sometimes reversible patterns of access and use. These findings suggest that engagement with I4.0 RIE is not driven by the availability of support alone, but by how managers interpret and position it in relation to their firms’ needs and constraints. By foregrounding these dynamics, the study offers a processual view of how SMEs engage with innovation ecosystems under digital transformation.

Title: “Will a robo-advisor help my grandpa?”: Exploring pathways to better integrate the elderly in the era of artificial intelligence
Authors: Roxana R. Iordache, Fernando A.F. Ferreira, Neuza C.M.Q.F. Ferreira, Marina Dabić, João J.M. Ferreira
Abstract: The global aging population, particularly the increasing number of individuals over 65 in Europe, presents both significant challenges and unique opportunities. This demographic shift has sparked the rise of the Silver Economy ( i.e. , a sector focused on the production, consumption and trade of goods and services aimed at improving the lives of the elderly), increasingly driven by technological solutions such as artificial intelligence (AI). Among these technologies, robo-advisors (RAs) hold promise in enhancing the quality of life, autonomy and social inclusion for older adults. However, while the potential of AI to integrate the elderly into society is widely acknowledged, there remain substantial gaps in understanding how best to deploy such technologies. Existing literature reveals critical limitations in methodologies and a lack of comprehensive models to guide the integration of AI into the lives of the elderly. This study addresses these gaps by adopting a constructivist approach and proposing a decision-support system to guide authorities in crafting effective policies and initiatives. The system is developed with input from field experts through participatory methods, specifically the Nominal Group Technique (NGT) and the DEcision MAking Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL), within a neutrosophic framework. By doing so, the study provides a more nuanced understanding of the barriers and opportunities in using RAs for the elderly, offering both theoretical advancements and practical recommendations to improve their integration into the AI-driven future of the Silver Economy.

Title: Openness and key core technology innovation: The moderating role of the interdisciplinary knowledge base
Abstract: The question of how openness affects firm innovation has long been complex and remains insufficiently explored. Drawing on an interdisciplinary knowledge base perspective, this study investigates how openness can be strategically managed to foster firms' key core technology (KCT) innovation. Using panel data from 177 listed firms in China's new energy vehicle (NEV) industry from 2000 to 2023, this study applies a zero-inflated negative binomial regression model to examine how the breadth and depth of openness influence KCT innovation, and how these effects are moderated by firms' interdisciplinary knowledge base. The results indicate that both the breadth and depth of openness exhibit inverted U-shaped relationships with KCT innovation, suggesting that moderate openness is most effective in promoting firms' KCT innovation. Furthermore, interdisciplinary knowledge diversity elevates the peak of the inverted U-shaped relationships for both openness breadth and depth and broadens their effective ranges, while interdisciplinary knowledge balance and disparity respectively attenuate the negative marginal effects of excessive openness breadth and depth. In sum, the study advances understanding of how to strategically manage innovation openness from an interdisciplinary knowledge base perspective to promote firms' KCT innovation, providing both theoretical contributions and practical guidance.

Title: Competition intensity and business model innovation: The distinctive role of strategic innovation readiness in European family and non-family SMEs
Authors: María-Mercedes Gracia-Laborda, Carolina López-Nicolás, Ángel-Luis Meroño-Cerdán
Abstract: This study proposes and tests a model that extends the knowledge of business model innovation (BMI)'s drivers, introducing strategic innovation readiness (SIR) as a fundamental mediating mechanism. Drawing on the Resource-Based View theory and the Socioemotional Wealth approach, we test the contingent effect of family firm on this model. Data were obtained from an international European Commission project to assess the relationships proposed. A sample of 417 Small and Medium-sized Enterprises was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The results indicate that competition intensity positively influences both BMI novelty and BMI scope, with SIR acting as a partial mediator in these relationships. A significant contribution of our multigroup analysis is that the indirect effect of competition intensity on BMI via SIR is stronger in non-family SMEs than in family SMEs. In addition, for non-family firms, SIR fully mediates the competition intensity-BMI scope relationship, whereas for family firms, this mediation is partial. These findings underscore that while both firm types need SIR to innovate, non-family firms exhibit a more pronounced and fully mediated response in broadening their BMI, suggesting distinct strategic pathways driven by inherent firm characteristics. These insights advance the BMI literature, particularly concerning the unique innovation dynamics of family versus non-family firms.

Title: Acceptance begins with understanding: Technology acceptance of autonomous and uncrewed vehicle systems in urban mobility and logistics
Authors: Clare McTigue, Emine Zehra Akgün, Luca Mora
Abstract: Urban mobility and logistics are being transformed by the adoption of autonomous and uncrewed vehicle systems (UxVs), yet research on user acceptance remains theoretically fragmented and empirically inconsistent. This study systematically reviews empirical research on UxV acceptance, across ground-based autonomous mobility technologies and autonomous logistics and last-mile delivery systems, excluding speculative aerial passenger technologies for which no empirical evidence exists. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), its subsequent extensions (TAM2, TAM3, and TAM for Smart Technologies), as well as the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT and UTAUT2), the review synthesises psychological, social, technological, and contextual determinants of UxV acceptance. Our analysis shows that acceptance arises from the multidimensional interaction of these factors and that no single model fully captures the domain-specific differences between mobility and logistics applications. Contextual influences, such as exogenous shock, organisational dynamics, and institutional and policy frameworks, appear as important moderators that shape, rather than replace, established TAM and UTAUT constructs. The review also identifies significant knowledge gaps, including the influence of socio-demographic variables, the need for technology-specific studies, and the importance of empirical research grounded in real-world trials. Addressing these gaps is essential to advancing theory and informing the effective integration of UxV technologies in complex urban environments.

Title: Crowdfunding success in digital platform-based entrepreneurial ecosystems: A configurational model of entrepreneur types and platform design
Abstract: Digital platforms have substantially transformed traditional entrepreneurial ecosystems by introducing new business models and opportunities for entrepreneurs to develop complementary products and services. Grounded in entrepreneurial ecosystem studies, digital platform practices, and entrepreneurial behavior theory, we propose a renewed theoretical framework to explain how platform design functions create framed entrepreneurial opportunities, and how entrepreneurs pursue their goals under standardized rules. We apply the fsQCA method to identify successful configurations of platform functions across different types of entrepreneurs based on crowdfunding campaigns from the Indiegogo platform. The findings reveal that novice entrepreneurs tend to adopt a visual strategy, relying on emotional resonance to achieve funding success. Cross-category habitual entrepreneurs are more adept at mobilizing social networks and incentive mechanisms, forming a social strategy. Non-cross-category habitual entrepreneurs, in contrast, depend on well-structured and coherent textual narratives to implement a linguistic strategy. These findings uncover a coupling relationship between platform design functions and entrepreneur types, suggesting that success is not determined by the number of functions used, but by the fit between platform design and entrepreneurs’ capabilities. Our research contributes to both entrepreneurial behavior theory and entrepreneurial ecosystem studies, and offers practical implications for how platforms can tailor differentiated support for various types of entrepreneurs.

Title: The innovation ripple effect of government venture capital: Dual-path diffusion via demonstration-learning and escape competition
Authors: Xu Wang, Wenyong Zhou, Jingen Zhou
Abstract: While extant research has demonstrated the positive impact of government venture capital (GVC) on innovation within its portfolio firms, the externalities exerted on local peers (defined as unfunded firms operating in the same city and industry sector as the portfolio firms) remain underexplored. To address this research gap, this study analyzes 23,164 GVC investment events in China from 2008 to 2023 and construct city–industry investment shocks to investigate this external effect. We find that GVC entry significantly enhances local peers' innovation performance, generating a distinct innovation ripple effect. Mechanism analysis reveals that this effect operates through two complementary channels: a demonstration-learning effect, whereby local peers learn from GVC-backed benchmarks to reduce innovation uncertainty, and an escape competition effect, which motivates peers to innovate under intensified market pressure. Notably, digital transformation strengthens of both mechanisms by enhancing local peers’ information-processing capacity and resource allocation flexibility. Further analysis indicates that the ripple effect is strongest among local peers with larger firms or those with higher total factor productivity (TFP), in more competitive or high-tech industries, and when GVC targets mature or non-state-owned enterprises (non-SOEs). These findings advance the understanding of GVC from a firm-level financing instrument to an ecosystem-restructuring innovation shock, enrich theories of policy-induced peer effects, and offer practical implications for cluster-level industrial upgrading.

Title: Goal versus duty? Persuading seniors to use generative AI-enabled medical applications
Authors: Changze Li, Yunkai Zhai, Jie Zhao, Mengran Xiong, Pan Gao, Tian Cheng, Yichuan Wang
Abstract: The integration of generative AI into healthcare presents a profound trust dilemma for older adults, a demographic highly sensitive to risk and algorithmic opacity. While existing literature primarily focuses on post-adoption AI interaction design, it largely overlooks the critical pre-adoption phase: how strategic marketing communication persuades vulnerable populations to engage with AI. Addressing this gap, this study investigates how marketing communication orientations: goal-oriented (emphasizing instrumental performance) versus duty-oriented (emphasizing safety and ethical governance) shape older adults’ trust and intention to adopt medical AI. Across three scenario-based experiments, we test a comprehensive behavioral model. Study 1 establishes a critical boundary condition, demonstrating that duty-oriented messaging significantly increases adoption intentions and trustworthiness in abstract, high-uncertainty preventive contexts, whereas this advantage diminishes in concrete, outcome-focused diagnostic and treatment settings. Studies 2 and 3 probe the underlying attributional mechanisms and individual differences by testing corporate motive attributions, AI literacy, and AI risk perception. Our findings reveal that duty-oriented framing enhances values-driven motive attributions, which in turn increase trust and adoption intentions among older adults. Furthermore, the persuasive advantage of duty-oriented communication is amplified for seniors with higher AI literacy. This study contributes to the digital innovation literature by shifting the paradigm from algorithmic interaction design to pre-adoption strategic framing and motive attribution. We provide actionable guidelines for practitioners to embed duty and normative transparency into their marketing to bridge the generative AI adoption gap for older adults.

Title: Internationalization or localization? The impact of U.S.-China technological decoupling on Chinese enterprises’ knowledge acquisition
Authors: Jiaying Liu, Yutao Sun, Yaqin Guo, Meng Cui
Abstract: National protectionism and unilateralism have continued to spread around the world. In particular, the U.S.-China technological decoupling has brought huge economic policy uncertainty to Chinese enterprises and has also profoundly affected their innovation. In this study, we develop a framework for how technological decoupling guides enterprises' knowledge acquisition: internationalization or localization. We use the differences-in-differences (DID) method to study why and how the technological decoupling affects enterprises' knowledge acquisition proxied by patent backward citations. Further, we also explore the heterogeneous effects of the enterprise's proximity to science and state ownership. Our analysis shows that the U.S.-China technological decoupling has reduced Chinese enterprises' knowledge acquisition from the U.S. This result does not exhibit spillover effects to other countries but rather reverse intense effects to own country, and Chinese enterprises affected by technological decoupling have acquired more local knowledge. Heterogeneity analysis results indicate that the effects of technological decoupling leading to a decrease in U.S. knowledge acquisition are more concentrated in enterprises proximity to science and non-state-owned enterprises (SOEs), whereas enterprises with a low degree of proximity and non-SOEs are significantly more impacted in local knowledge acquisition. By redirecting innovation outcomes towards knowledge acquisition, our findings enrich the literature on the impact of technological decoupling on innovation, aiding in the comprehension of changes in enterprise innovation behavior from a technological decoupling perspective.

Title: Inclusion 4.0: How industry 4.0 drives workforce inclusion of people with disabilities
Authors: Gonzalo Fernandez, Jéssica de Assis Dornelles, Néstor Fabián Ayala
Abstract: The integration of Industry 4.0 technologies into manufacturing systems has largely emphasized productivity and efficiency, with limited attention to how the inclusion of people with disabilities (PwD) can contribute to and reshape these performance outcomes. Addressing this gap, this study investigates how Industry 4.0 technologies can support workers with sensory and physical disabilities within manufacturing environments. The research employs a qualitative methodology, combining semi-structured interviews with professionals from multinational corporations and specialists in this field as well as analysis of corporate reports to evaluate the effects of technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), collaborative robots (cobots), augmented reality (AR), and exoskeletons in workers inclusion. Findings reveal that these technologies generate upskilling (e.g., AI-enhanced assistive devices for visual impairments), reskilling (e.g., learning how to do quality inspections with multisensory feedback provided by IoT sensors for hearing impairments), and deskilling (e.g., cobot-assisted task simplification for physical disabilities), depending on the disability type and context. The study introduces the concept of “Inclusion 4.0″, positioning Industry 4.0 as a catalyst for equitable workforce participation aligned with the Industry 5.0 human-centric pillar. Practical implications include actionable insights for policymakers and managers to design inclusive industrial systems, while theoretical contributions highlight a socio-technical framework that prioritizes disability-inclusive technological adoption.

Title: AI capability and labor productivity in low- and middle-income countries: An absorptive capacity approach
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between national AI capability and labor productivity in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) through the lens of absorptive capacity theory. Rather than focusing on frontier AI innovation, we conceptualize AI capability as a transformation-stage construct emerging from the interaction between AI-embodied external inflows (e.g., AI-related hardware imports) and domestic complementary conditions (e.g., internet penetration, broadband access, electricity access, and financial inclusion). This framing reflects how most LMICs engage with AI—through embodied technology imports combined with enabling structural conditions. Using a panel dataset of 63 LMICs over the period 2005–2019, we construct a novel AI Capability Index via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and estimate its association with labor productivity using two-way fixed effects and system GMM estimators. We complement this analysis with interaction-based specifications that separate AI-related inflows and domestic readiness conditions and examine how their interaction relates to labor productivity. Our results reveal a robust and statistically significant positive association: a one standard deviation increase in AI capability is associated with approximately a 9.20–9.37% increase in labor productivity, depending on index construction (flow-based vs. stock-based). Results remain stable across alternative specifications and sensitivity analyses. These findings indicate that productivity gains in LMICs depend not solely on access to AI-related technologies, but also on the complementary institutional and infrastructural conditions that enable their transformation and diffusion. By operationalizing AI capability as a national-level transformation-stage construct, this study extends absorptive capacity theory beyond the firm level and provides a replicable empirical framework for assessing national AI capability formation and its relationship to labor productivity under data-constrained conditions. In doing so, it contributes to ongoing debates on digital transformation, technological adoption, and capability formation in LMICs.

Title: Predicting Local Innovation through AI and geospatial models: Revisiting the Innovation District Theory
Abstract: This paper aims to deepen the understanding of variations in innovation performance across neighbourhoods within a city. Specifically, the study investigates the characteristics that influence innovation generation at the sub-city level to provide insights that would bridge the gap between national, regional, and local innovation policies. It aims to revisit the traditional Innovation District Theory in the post-AI era by proposing an innovation district model that shifts the focus from supply chains to innovation diffusion, moving beyond characterizing innovation districts solely by business metrics. To do it, we leverage an empirically merged dataset to explore well-established and newly introduced enabling factors of innovation generation. First, we employ a random forest algorithm to predict innovation performance using patent data from the census zip code tabulation areas (ZCTAs) across the New York metro area. This approach highlights significant neighbourhood assets associated with high innovation performance. Secondly, machine learning and deep learning models are trained and tested on ZCTAs from New York state with high predictive accuracy. Our findings show that when trained with neighbourhood assets and tested on New York state ZCTAs demonstrate high predictive accuracy, explaining 60% to 70% of the variation in innovation performance ten years later using specific neighbourhood asset variables. Additionally, when trained on data from the New York central metro area tested on data from Boston's central metro area, the accuracy remains relatively stable, suggesting an association between the assessed neighbourhood assets and innovation performance across these two US central metro areas. In the end, we introduce a newly constructed index, the Local Innovation Potential (LIP), designed to a neighbourhood’s innovation potential over the same period, in both states. These results reinforce the importance of key early neighbourhood-level characteristics strongly associated with high long-term innovation performance and provide a tool with practical implications for urban planning as well as for innovation policy design and implementation.

Title: Auditing AI systems: Integrating ESG principles for sustainable and ethical AI deployment in the EU
Authors: Cinzia Colapinto, Chiara Galimberti, Marco Repetto
Abstract: The European Union Artificial Intelligence Act establishes a framework to ensure that artificial intelligence systems deployed within the European Union are safe, compliant with fundamental rights, and aligned with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles. However, it lacks specific guidelines to address ESG trade-offs, such as balancing transparency with fairness or environmental concerns with societal impact. This article introduces a novel artificial intelligence audit framework that integrates ESG criteria using the Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchical Approach and Multicriteria Optimization. The framework acts as an institutional translation mechanism and enables decision-makers to prioritize ESG trade-offs and optimally allocate limited resources. By systematically identifying, prioritizing, and addressing the risks of the artificial intelligence system, the framework enhances innovation governance and ensures sustainable and ethical deployment of artificial intelligence. Applying this framework results in improved audit quality, enhanced risk mitigation, and continuous improvement of artificial intelligence systems, thereby promoting positive societal and environmental outcomes. This integrated framework bridges the gap between regulatory expectations and practical implementation, fostering responsible innovation in artificial intelligence in the European Union. Overall, we contribute to the extant literature by repositioning AI governance from a compliance-oriented activity to a dynamic capability that enables firms to manage ESG trade-offs and sustain responsible AI innovation under regulatory uncertainty.

Title: The venture clienting readiness canvas: How corporations can assess their organizational readiness for new venture collaboration
Authors: Bugra Kilinc, Konstantin Remke, Leonard Brütting
Abstract: Venture clienting (VCL) emerged as an increasingly prominent form of collaboration between corporations and new ventures. However, many VCL initiatives stall because corporations are not organizationally prepared to collaborate with new ventures. Using a design science (DS) methodology, this study introduces the Venture Clienting Readiness Canvas, an ex-ante assessment tool that helps corporations evaluate the internal conditions necessary for successful VCL before engagement begins.
