We derived five readiness domains—strategic alignment, collaboration governance, communication and trust, organizational culture, and collaboration processes—from a systematic literature review. In addition, we refined the canvas through four practitioner workshops with experienced VCL experts as part of a formative evaluation and subsequently assessed the artifact in a summative evaluation involving nine additional VCL practitioners. The results demonstrate that the canvas offers a structured, actionable approach to assessing organizational readiness for VCL. Thus, this study contributes prescriptive design knowledge on how corporations can anticipate the organizational tensions, coordination demands, and organizational change necessities inherent in collaborating with new ventures.

Title: Multinational enterprises and strategic foresight: The path to eco-innovation
Authors: Coralie Gagné, Sophie Veilleux, Fabiano Armellini, Elicia Maine, Carole Lalonde, Catherine Beaudry
Abstract: This study applies neo-institutional theory and dynamic capability theory to an aerospace multinational case study for examining how firms can plan for eco-innovation through strategic foresight and how such planning shapes and is shaped by the institutional environment. The findings show that strategic foresight enables organisations to interpret institutional pressures and reconfigure dynamic capabilities to support eco-innovation. To ensure coherence and continuity, multinational enterprises (MNEs) should assign responsibility for eco-innovation to a dedicated unit, supported by collaboration across internal divisions and with customers. Foresight activities guide the introduction of eco-innovation initiatives and embed them into the daily operations of all units. Overall, this case study shows how policymaking processes, design dynamics, and societal demands can motivate an MNE to integrate eco-innovation across its organisation and clarifies the central role of strategic foresight. Large firms are shown to be pivotal actors in eco-innovation, influencing change within their internal units and across the entire value chain.

Title: Digital transformation, R&D internationalization, and corporate green innovation: Can they play a supportive role? Empirical evidence from China
Authors: Mengya Li, Ji Zou, Qian Ma, Chen Hao
Abstract: Green innovation has become a critical pathway through which firms can reconcile economic growth with environmental sustainability, particularly in emerging economies undergoing simultaneous digital and green transitions. Using panel data on Chinese listed manufacturing firms from 2015 to 2024, this study examines how the breadth and depth of R&D internationalization affect corporate green innovation and investigates how digital transformation (DT) conditions these relationships through distinct technological layers. The results show that both breadth and depth of R&D internationalization significantly promote green innovation. Breadth-oriented R&D internationalization promotes green innovation primarily by reducing firms' reliance on slack resources and improving operational efficiency, whereas depth-oriented R&D internationalization enhances green innovation by increasing R&D efficiency and leveraging industry-level innovation spillovers. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the effects of R&D internationalization on green innovation are conditioned by DT in asymmetric ways. DT technology architecture, which enhances firms’ information-processing capacity and cross-border knowledge integration, strengthens the positive impact of R&D internationalization on green innovation. In contrast, DT technology application, which through intensified process embedding and routine reconfiguration, weakens these effects by inducing attention overload, process rigidity, and resource crowding-out. Supermodularity tests further show that DT technology architecture and R&D internationalization generally exhibit complementarity, whereas DT technology application systematically generates substitution effects. In addition, the crowding-out effect of DT technology application is stronger for higher-quality and more exploratory green innovation outcomes than for more incremental ones. This study advances a nuanced understanding of how DT reshapes the effectiveness of global R&D strategies for sustainability-oriented innovation and provides actionable insights for firms seeking to balance digital upgrading and green innovation under resource and capability constraints.

Title: Co-creating frugal innovation at the bottom of the pyramid
Authors: Mokter Hossain, Masoud Karami, Muhammad Shehryar Shahid, Nomah Javed, Samuel Adomako
Abstract: Frugal innovation, characterised by affordable, cost-effective, resource-efficient solutions, has become increasingly significant for addressing the needs of the Bottom of the Pyramid (BoP) in emerging markets. It necessitates concerted efforts by key stakeholders with the shared goal of co-creating new solutions to enhance the quality of life at the BoP. However, the exploration of co-creation in devising affordable solutions for the underserved BoP market is limited in the literature. This study explores how entrepreneurs collaborate with key stakeholders to co-create frugal innovations for the BoP customers in an emerging market. We employed a multiple case study approach to address the research question. Analyzing data from 12 start-ups, including 43 interviews, our findings revealed the collaboration mechanisms in the frugal innovation process addressing BOP needs. We also demonstrate how start-ups form collaborative networks co-create frugal innovations, overcoming multiple constraints by utilising shared resources, knowledge, and capabilities. Furthermore, we reveal the key outcomes of frugal innovations. The findings advance the frugal innovation literature by incorporating co-creation as a strategic approach to addressing innovation challenges at the BoP. We extend both co-creation and frugal innovation literature by stressing the significance of co-creation in identifying problems, understanding complex scenarios, and devising affordable solutions.

Title: Integrating sustainability with disruptive innovation: A comprehensive framework to identify key characteristics, barriers, and enablers
Abstract: This study develops a comprehensive framework for Sustainable Disruptive Innovations (SDIs) to address gaps in understanding how disruption can drive sustainability transitions. Although research on disruptive innovation and sustainability has advanced substantially, their integration remains limited and conceptually fragmented. Drawing on a systematic review of 53 studies and content analysis of 28 cases, we identify the core characteristics, barriers, and enablers that shape SDI emergence and scalability. Using the Sustainability Pillars Model, the framework explains how early niche entry, iterative value-proposition refinement, and the reconfiguration of value networks enable SDIs to progress toward broader adoption. We also distinguish user-driven and producer-driven SDIs, revealing how each follows different trajectories and confronts distinct constraints. The findings show that SDIs succeed when barrier–enabler dynamics support movement from early experimentation to system-level impact. The study extends disruption theory by demonstrating how sustainability considerations reshape innovation pathways and provides actionable insights for leveraging market disruption to advance the Sustainable Development Goals.

Title: Digital transformation and social sustainability: the mediating role of employees’ digital competencies
Authors: Mirta Díaz-Fernández, Juan Carlos Rivera-Prieto, Álvaro López-Cabrales
Abstract: Corporate Social Sustainability (CSS) has emerged as a cornerstone of contemporary organisational strategy. Indeed, the concept deliberately integrates equitable practices, employee empowerment, and community resilience into core operational frameworks. Digital transformation holds the potential to enhance CSS by fostering innovation, inclusivity, and operational efficiency; yet the process also presents risks, including labour displacement, data privacy concerns, and environmental challenges. This study examines how the digital competencies of employees mediate the relationship between digital transformation and CSS, drawing on the integration of the Resource-Based View and Stakeholder Theory to position these competencies as strategic organisational resources. The dual effects of digital transformation on CSS were unravelled based on longitudinal data from 452 publicly listed European firms collected over the 2015–2021 seven-year period as well as panel data techniques. The development of digital competencies proved to be essential to achieve CSS. Our findings contribute to the literature by demonstrating that employees’ digital competencies are a key mechanism through which digital transformation can be translated into socially sustainable outcomes. The combination of the Resource-Based View and Stakeholder Theory allowed clarifying how human capital capabilities enable firms to achieve social sustainability through digitalisation. The study findings offer organisations and policymakers actionable guidance for designing digital upskilling and inclusion strategies that effectively advance corporate sustainability goals.

Title: Understanding innovation in coopetitive contexts: A meta-analysis
Authors: Chuan Li, Xinwu He, Mark Palmer
Abstract: Research on coopetition suggests that cooperation and competition can jointly shape firm innovation outcomes. Central to this literature is the management of relational dynamics, reflected in the varying intensity of cooperation, competition, and their joint manifestation in coopetition. However, empirical findings remain inconclusive regarding the magnitude and contextual conditions under which relational dynamics, namely cooperation intensity, competition intensity, and coopetition intensity, relate to innovation outcomes. Informed by the coopetition paradox perspective and contingency logic, this study synthesises prior research by conducting a meta-analysis of 51 quantitative studies comprising 118,467 observations. The analysis estimates effect sizes for the relationships between relational dynamics and innovation outcomes and examines how these relationships vary across contextual and methodological characteristics. The results indicate that cooperation intensity and coopetition intensity are positively associated with innovation outcomes, whereas competition intensity does not show a consistent direct association across studies. Meta-regression analyses indicate that these relationships vary selectively across key contextual (e.g., industry type, geographic scope, and innovation radicalness) and methodological characteristics (e.g., measurement approach and unit of analysis). This study thus extends the coopetition–innovation literature by showing that coopetition is better understood not as a unified construct, but as distinct dimensions of relational dynamics whose associations with innovation outcomes vary across contexts.

Title: Actual technology use among older adults and its effects in an emerging country: Exploring life satisfaction and social inclusion
Authors: Khaled Saleh Al-Omoush, Miguel Angel Millan Atenciano, Samuel Ribeiro-Navarrete, Marcin W. Staniewski
Abstract: Older adults (OAs) are among the groups most affected by the demands of digital transformation, as they encounter greater barriers to adopting technology compared with other age groups. This empirical study examines how the perceptions of OAs influence their actual technology use and subsequently how this use affects their well-being and social life. A questionnaire was administered to 206 OAs. Smart PLS software facilitated data analysis. The results revealed that perceived value, perceived cognitive load, and facilitating conditions significantly impact actual technology use among OAs. Actual technology use was also found to have a significant impact on life satisfaction and social inclusion. Moreover, social support strongly moderates the association between actual technology use and both life satisfaction and social inclusion. This study makes a significant theoretical contribution by investigating the intersection of technology, aging, satisfaction, and social interaction. The study integrates diverse cognitive, environmental, and social factors into a novel framework explaining technology use among OAs. The findings also offer substantial practical value for policymakers, health and social service providers, and technology designers, seeking to improve the quality of life and reduce social isolation among OAs.

Title: Understanding the determinants of older adults’ adoption of AI-powered wearable devices: The moderating and mediating role of health consciousness and attitude
Authors: Veland Ramadani, Barış Armutcu, Ahmet Tan, Mehmet Aytekin, Sadudin Ibraimi
Abstract: Purpose: This study examines the factors influencing older adults' adoption of AI-powered wearable devices (AIWD) and aims to develop strategies to promote the effective use of these technologies among the aging population. To provide a comprehensive explanation of adoption behaviour, this study integrates Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and the theory of planned behaviour (TPB). Specifically, it investigates the effects of SDT components (competence, relatedness, and autonomy) and TAM components (perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use) on older adults’ attitudes toward AI-powered wearable devices, as well as the effects of attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control on the intention to use. In addition, the mediating role of attitude and the moderating role of health consciousness were examined. Design/methodology/approach: Data were collected from older adults through a structured questionnaire administered by a professional survey company. To reduce potential common method bias, procedural remedies were applied, and statistical controls were conducted. The proposed research model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). Finding: - The results indicate that competence, relatedness, autonomy, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use have significant positive effects on attitudes toward AI-powered wearable devices. Attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control significantly influenced the intention to use AIWD. Health consciousness has a significant direct effect on the intention to use, but does not moderate the relationship between attitude and intention. Mediation analysis revealed that attitude plays a significant mediating role in the relationships between relatedness, autonomy, perceived ease of use, and intention to use, whereas no mediating effect was found for competence and perceived usefulness. Overall, the findings highlight the central role of attitude, along with social and behavioural factors, in older adults’ adoption of wearable AI technologies. Implications: This study provides practical insights for technology developers, healthcare professionals, and policymakers seeking to facilitate the adoption of AI-powered wearable devices among older adults. Originality/value: This study offers an integrated theoretical perspective and contributes to the literature by examining older adults’ adoption of AI-powered wearable devices in the context of a rapidly aging developing country.

Title: From a notorious companion to the ruler of the world: future scenarios of AI development from the perspective of science fiction movies
Abstract: AI is an emerging technology that is rapidly advancing, and understanding its future is highly uncertain. Therefore, linear approaches and forecasts based only on past trends cannot provide a holistic image of the future. Therefore, in this study, we used scenario planning to deal with the aforementioned uncertainties and to explore alternative futures of artificial intelligence (AI) development. To follow a structured and coherent approach, we adopted the Global Business Network (GBN) method of scenario planning that is well known due to its systematic framework, i.e., identification of key drivers, critical uncertainties, and narratives of alternative futures. To overcome the limitations of the GBN method, including heavy reliance on experts' judgment, demarcating imagination within common mental frameworks, and overlooking some aspects of the future, we adjusted its steps to tailor it for science fiction (Sci-Fi) content as an input for proposing alternative futures of AI. Sci-Fi movies, compared to the conventional sources of scenario planning, reflect and depict collective imaginations, social concerns, and alternative views about the future of a technology in a different manner. By reviewing the literature and reports pertinent to the future of AI, we identified six drivers shaping AI's development. Among them, we selected three key uncertainties, including social acceptance, singularity, and regulation. By combining different states of these uncertainties, we captured four plausible and six possible scenarios from a corpus of 63 selected Sci-Fi movies and series. By integrating the GBN method with media scanning of Sci-Fi content, our proposed scenarios describe alternative future states of AI development, ranging from AI as a destructive entity to a symbiotic being or a personal companion. Four plausible scenarios cover a utopian, a dystopian, and two in-between futures. Our findings imply that four common future application areas of AI are military and security, simulation of human interactions, entertainment, and services. Without proper regulation, military and security applications of AI may pose risks to societies. At the firm level, our results provide insights into future frontiers and hybrid AI technologies that may be of use to managers and policymakers. Our scenarios suggest that ethical and social aspects of AI, both at the firm and at the national level, are key factors in shaping the future of AI development, which should be carefully considered.

Title: Organizational learning and digitalization capability: Evidence from Chinese SMEs in dynamic environments
Authors: Guomeng Zheng, Qianwen Wang, Yu Qin, Zhiyong Zhang, Baofeng Huo, Mengxi Guo
Abstract: Organizational learning plays a pivotal role in enhancing the digitalization capabilities of SMEs, encompassing both foundational digital infrastructure and advanced digital analysis, but the precise mechanisms underlying their relationship remain underexplored, especially in the increasingly dynamic environments. Drawing upon dynamic capability theory (DCT), this study develops a moderated mediation model to investigate how fundamental digital infrastructure mediates the relationship between organization learning (e.g., internal and external learning) and advanced digital analysis, as well as market and industry environment (e.g., environmental complexity and competition intensity) as moderators between organization learning and digitalization capability. Using the data collected from 887 Chinese SMEs, the findings reveal that organizational learning is positively related to fundamental digital infrastructure and advanced digital analysis, in which fundamental digital infrastructure serves as a mediating mechanism linking organizational learning to advanced digital analysis. Regarding contextual influences, environmental complexity weakens the relationship between internal learning and fundamental digital infrastructure, while strengthening the relationship between external learning and fundamental digital infrastructure. Competitive intensity strengthens the relationship between internal learning and fundamental digital infrastructure but weakens that between external learning and fundamental digital infrastructure. These moderating effects do not generally extend to advanced digital analysis. The study enhances the understanding of the factors shaping digitalization capabilities in SMEs while also revealing the opportunities and challenges of the market and industry environment.

Title: Extending the potential of venture creation programmes for the commercialisation of research-based technologies
Authors: Thi Thanh Thuy Do, Øystein Widding, Dag Håkon Haneberg, Manuela Cirilli, Torgeir Aadland, Giovanni Anelli
Abstract: This paper explores the processes undertaken by students in a venture creation programme (VCP) who engage in early-stage technology commercialisation of research-based technologies provided by external institutions. Our research question is: How can VCPs support students in the commercialisation of research-based technologies? We conducted a process study of a spinoff company that is based on a technology developed at the European Organisation for Nuclear Research (CERN). Facilitated by a VCP and through a formal agreement with an external research institution, it is possible for novice students to identify and create opportunities within a complex and uncertain context, including a highly advanced technological field. Guided by a process study approach, the paper conceptualised the sequence of events during the students’ entrepreneurial process. The paper builds on the conceptual frame of reference that VCPs combine several approaches to supporting entrepreneurship and commercialisation at universities. Thus, it contributes to the literature on research commercialisation processes with insights into the processual micro-foundations of overcoming challenges and junctures in the commercialisation process. We suggest that involving VCP students represents an alternative model of technology commercialisation in high-cost economies that fosters fruitful collaboration among the VCP, VCP students and researchers.

Title: From green inventions to products: The role of firm and policy alignment in product integration
Abstract: Green innovation is critical to sustainability, yet many green inventions do not make it into products. In this study, we argue that integrating green inventions into products poses distinct appropriability challenges. Accordingly, the alignment of an invention's technological domains, both with the firm's prior inventive activities (firm alignment) and with public R&D funding priorities (policy alignment), may matter more for the product integration of green inventions than for the product integration of non-green inventions. Using data on the product integration outcomes of 2160 patented inventions from a European automotive firm, we find that firm alignment is more strongly associated with product integration for green inventions than for non-green inventions. We find no clear evidence of a similar pattern for policy alignment. These findings highlight product integration as a key downstream organizational process in green innovation and clarify how firm and policy alignment relate to green inventions' product integration.

Title: Exploration versus exploitation: The innovation propensity of academic spin-offs during the sustainable returns phase
Authors: Yijia Dai, Jing Xu, Yang Ye
Abstract: Academic spin-offs (ASOs) are widely recognized for their innovation premium, originating from the transfer of novel academic knowledge and superior innovative capacities. However, their innovation patterns after achieving the sustainable returns phase remain underexplored. To understand the temporal dynamics of their innovation strategies, we focus on mature ASOs using a sample of Chinese publicly listed firms from 2008 to 2020. We find that mature ASOs exhibit a stronger propensity for exploitative innovation over exploratory innovation when compared with their non-academic counterparts. Moreover, this tendency is amplified by greater external institutional investment, but mitigated by a greater proportion of non-academic team members and greater internal financial slack. Overall, this study advances research on ASO innovation by clarifying how ASOs leverage their innovative advantage in the sustainable returns phase, as well as highlighting the continuing importance of commercial resources in shaping mature ASOs’ innovation propensity.

Title: AI-powered innovation tournament evaluations: A hybrid NLP approach
Authors: Rafael Luiz Velôzo Santiago, Isis Didier Lins
Abstract: Innovation tournaments require expert evaluators to assess large volumes of lengthy, unstructured proposals under significant time pressure and cognitive constraints. This study investigates how transformer-based natural language processing (NLP) models can be integrated into this context as decision-support tools within the evaluation process. Using real-world data from a national Brazilian innovation tournament comprising 1151 startup proposals, we examine whether NLP models can learn patterns associated with expert-assigned scores and support early-stage screening. We fine-tune Portuguese-language transformer models (BERT) for classification tasks and refine long-text processing through chunking and document-level aggregation. To contextualize performance, we benchmark the neural models against lighter architectures and classical machine-learning baselines. Although the models exhibit persistent ambiguity in distinguishing intermediate-quality proposals, the best-performing configuration consistently avoids extreme misclassifications and adopts a conservative screening profile that prioritizes the retention of high-potential submissions.

Title: Corrigendum to “Digital transformation and social sustainability: the mediating role of employees’ digital competencies” [Technovation 156 (2026) 103607]
Authors: Mirta Diaz-Fernandez, Juan Carlos Rivera-Prieto, Alvaro Lopez-Cabrales

Authors: Xiaobin Zhang, Mengxi Yang, Yimei Hu, Yongwei Wang, Weijie Wu
Abstract: The authors regret that the funding information in the published article contained an incorrect grant number. Title: Big data analytics, resource bundling, and firm performance: The dual impacts of servitization
Abstract: Despite substantial investments in big data analytics by manufacturing firms, how these investments translate into business value remains poorly understood. Drawing on resource orchestration theory (ROT) and insights from the big data literature, we examine how improving resource bundling (IRB) and pioneering resource bundling (PRB) mediate the impact of big data analytics on firm performance and the moderating role of servitization in these relationships. Analyzing a dataset of 322 Chinese manufacturers, we find that both IRB and PRB serve as mediators for the positive effect of big data analytics on firm performance. Interestingly, servitization strengthens the positive relationship between big data analytics and IRB while weakening its positive relationship with PRB, illustrating a double-edged effect. This study advances the literature in several streams, including big data analytics, servitization, and resource orchestration.

Title: Twin transition in manufacturing firms: The role of supply chain orchestration and supply chain business model innovation
Authors: Debadrita Panda, Vinit Parida, Johan Frishammar
Abstract: Twin transition, the concurrent development of digitalization practices and circular practices, are believed to be the key to firm performance. However, empirical evidence is currently scarce regarding the effect of twin transition on firm performance and the complementary practices that enable and realize it. This study draws on a survey of 188 Swedish manufacturing firms and employs PLS structural equation modelling to test the hypothesis. The results indicate that firm performance can be improved through digitalization practices but with circular practices as a mediator. Moreover, our results show a significant and positive moderation effect of supply chain orchestration and supply chain business model innovation as complementary mechanisms for enabling and realizing the process. This implies time sequencing between the two twin transition dimensions. These results carry theoretical implications for twin transition research and circular economy literatures. The results also provide novel managerial insights by showing that digital investments must be coupled with early orchestration of supply chain partners and aligned business model innovation to effectively scale circular practices and realize performance benefits.

Title: Digital technology adoption and servitization of manufacturing firms —The role of knowledge coupling and collaborative network cohesion
Authors: Jing Ning, Wei Li, Yahui Xu, Baozhou Lu
Abstract: In the current digital era, manufacturing firms are increasingly pursuing servitization to enhance competitive advantage. Nevertheless, the mechanisms linking digital technology adoption (DTA) to servitization remain underexplored. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities perspective (DCP) and ecosystem perspective, this study develops a conceptual model to examine how DTA is associated with servitization through knowledge coupling and under what conditions this relationship is amplified or constrained. Utilizing data from 925 listed Chinese manufacturing firms over the 2010–2024 period, we employ a two-way fixed effects model to show that DTA is positively associated with servitization, with knowledge coupling serving as a critical mediating pathway. Furthermore, we identify that collaborative network cohesion plays an inverted U-shaped moderating role on the DTA–knowledge coupling relationship, highlighting the importance of an optimally structured ecosystem for effective knowledge integration. These findings advance theoretical understanding of digital-enabled servitization and provide actionable insights for managers seeking to leverage digital technologies and ecosystem networks to facilitate service-oriented transformation.

Title: Beyond the surface: Exploring configurations for digital innovation based on digital technology affordance theory
Abstract: In the digital era, as enterprises increasingly embrace a variety of digital technologies to drive innovation and alleviate operational pressures, the key challenge has evolved from simple technology adoption to the strategic selection and integration of these technologies for achieving optimal results. Although previous literature has examined the factors contributing to heterogeneous digital innovation outcomes, most studies focusing on the independent effects of these factors fail to fully capture the causal complexity underlying digital innovation. Drawing on digital technology affordance theory, this study addresses this gap by adopting a configurational approach based on the “Technology-Organization-Goal” (T-O-G) framework. Using data from 2151 listed manufacturing companies in China that participate in digital innovation, the study employs fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to identify configurations that generate high levels of digital innovation. The findings demonstrate that differences in innovation performance do not arise from isolated factors, but from the actualization of affordances enabled by the synergistic alignment of technology, organization, and goals. Crucially, we show that affordance actualization is not an automatic outcome but hinges on specific configurations. Furthermore, we highlight that the conversion of technological potential into value is strictly governed by the alignment between an organization's structural attributes and its strategic intent. Finally, by revealing equifinal pathways to successful digital innovation rather than a one-size-fits-all solution, our findings provide managers with actionable guidance.

Title: Platform Thinking in Action: A design science research to bring the platform revolution in legacy firms
Abstract: Digital platforms have become a dominant logic for value creation and innovation, yet legacy firms still struggle to translate platform principles into actionable organizational transformation. A central reason is cognitive: managers often mis-frame platforms as digital services rather than as ecosystem-based value architectures. This paper adopts a Design Science approach to develop and refine the Platform Thinking Journey, a composite managerial artifact that supports platform transformation in incumbent firms. Developed through a three-year, multi-firm collaboration within the Platform Thinking HUB, the artifact evolved across three iterative waves from exploratory tools into a validated journey structured around four phases: Framing, Design, Ignition, and Growth. The resulting Platform Thinking Journey combines a process model, bounded decision cycles, and an integrated physical and digital, or “phygital”, support architecture, including cards, canvases, workshops, digital templates, and a GenAI co-thinker. Its core mechanism is to make platform theory actionable by presenting structured alternatives grounded in the literature, focusing managerial attention, reducing ambiguity, and aligning interpretation before teams consolidate choices through design tools and milestones. The study contributes to platform and innovation management research by showing how platform transformation can be actively supported through design, and by identifying five design principles for incumbent firms: reframing from products to interactions before solutioning, structuring the process as bounded decision cycles, materializing reasoning through boundary objects, balancing conceptual depth with cognitive manageability, and sustaining reflection through phygital continuity. Methodologically, the paper offers a rigorous application of Design Science to a non-technical managerial artifact in a multi-wave, multi-firm collaborative setting. For managers, the Platform Thinking Journey provides a structured way to reframe platform opportunities, make key design choices explicit, and sustain reflection across the transformation process.

Title: How do university–industry collaboration models evolve and get selected in industrial parks?
Authors: Jun Liu, Xuewei Wang, Wenqing Miao, Xiurong Wang
Abstract: Industrial parks have become important sites for university–industry collaboration (UIC), yet existing research offers limited explanation of why particular UIC models emerge, evolve, and work unevenly across institutional contexts. This study develops a hierarchical multi-level framework in which field embeddedness shapes institutional linkages and Actor Endowments, which in turn condition UIC model selection. Using survey data from 412 respondents across 16 Chinese industrial parks and comparative case evidence from four focal parks, supplemented by RTP as an international reference, we identify four analytically ordered UIC models: talent exchange, technology transfer, value co-creation, and ecosystem symbiosis. The SEM results show that Actor Endowments exert the strongest direct association with UIC model selection (β = 0.482, p < 0.001), whereas field embeddedness operates mainly through indirect pathways via institutional linkages and Actor Endowments. These mechanisms vary across park types and regional development levels. The study contributes to UIC research by explaining model differentiation and progressive upgrading through a contextualized multi-level framework, offering implications for policy, park management, and collaborative practice.

Title: Supportive or exhausting: How resources synergize in network embedding innovation process to improve sustainability
Authors: Qin Liu, Ruming Chen, Xiaonan Wen, De Xia
Abstract: As sustainability improvement becomes increasingly complex and uncertain, firms are increasingly dependent on networked innovation capability to integrate dispersed knowledge and technologies from external entities. However, the transformation from networked innovation capability to sustainability involves a procedural mechanism that requires effective synergy among limited multidimensional financial and digital resources. This procedural mechanism and the role of resource synergy within it remain underexplored. Based on network embeddedness theory, innovation value chain theory, and resource synergy theory, this study constructs an integrated “Networked Innovation Capabilities-Process-Resources” synergy framework and employs stepwise regression analysis on a sample of 165 new energy vehicle firms. Results show that: (1) Networked knowledge innovation capability promotes sustainability through a procedural mechanism involving networked technology innovation capability and market value. (2) Multidimensional financial resources exert heterogeneous effects across different links of the procedural mechanism, with financial leverage and profitability showing significantly positive moderating effects, while operational efficiency shows no significant effect. (3) Multidimensional digital resources exert dual supportive or exhausting influences on the synergistic effects of financial resources, where digital development orientation provides consistent support, whereas digital software and hardware investment exhibit both supportive and exhausting effects contingent upon the specific link of the procedural mechanism. This study elucidates how networked innovation capability affects sustainability through a procedural mechanism and how diverse yet limited resources synergize in this process. It provides theoretical and practical insights for firms and governments to promote networked innovation capability and optimize the allocation of financial and digital resources in innovation process for sustainability.

Title: From hammers to toolkits: A methodological framework for applying design science to orchestrating collaborative innovation processes
Abstract: Collaborative innovation is crucial in addressing complex challenges such as sustainability-oriented and technological transformation. While previous research has explored the mechanisms and outcomes of collaborative innovation, scholars and practitioners still lack clear, actionable guidance on how to design, select, adapt, and evaluate the tools and methods—referred to as artifacts—that support the collaborative innovation process. This paper addresses that question. Drawing on an Action Design Research (ADR) study across three cases and five iterative build-intervene-evaluate cycles, we develop the Orchestrating Collaborative Innovation (OCI) methodological framework. Grounded in a process perspective, organization theory, and empirical insights, OCI introduces 18 phase-specific design principles for innovation community participants and 10 for orchestrators to guide artifact development. OCI is a methodological framework for design science scholars and innovation orchestrators. It supports scholars and practitioners in designing, adapting, and selecting artifacts that align with a specific phase of the collaborative innovation process and evaluating them accordingly. By doing so, the innovation community can become more cohesive, align on shared goals, and co-create innovation. Beyond collaborative innovation, the framework contributes to advancing a process perspective in design science by emphasising the evolving, relational, and performative nature of the innovation process.

Title: Reverse engineering, rapid validity testing, and digital product innovation in emerging market firms
Authors: Qilong Zong, Guohong Wang, Huan Lin, Hao Huang
Abstract: While reverse engineering is widely recognized as a key mechanism for emerging market firms to acquire sophisticated knowledge for product innovation, it faces distinctive challenges when applied to digital products due to their layered modular architecture. Substantial portions of digital product functionality reside in unobservable layers such as algorithms, data, and backend services, limiting the completeness of knowledge that reverse engineering can capture. Drawing on layered modular architecture literature, we propose that rapid validity testing serves as an important bridging mechanism that transforms the incomplete knowledge from reverse engineering into more comprehensive and actionable insights for digital product innovation. Using multi-wave survey data from 286 Chinese manufacturing firms, we find that reverse engineering is positively associated with digital product innovation in emerging market firms, and rapid validity testing mediates this relationship. We also find that the indirect effect is positively moderated by firms’ knowledge integration capability. This study advances understanding of how emerging market firms leverage acquired architectural knowledge to overcome the observability constraints commonly encountered in digital product innovation, and illuminates the organizational processes through which such knowledge is transformed into genuine innovation capability.

Title: Do digital M&As drive higher acquisition premiums? Evidence from Chinese listed firms
Authors: Qiongyu Huang, Jiali Fang, Wenqi Han, Yonggen Luo
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between digital mergers and acquisitions (M&As) and acquisition premiums in the context of China's rapidly evolving digital economy. Based on 4761 acquisition events of A-share listed firms from 2011 to 2022, we find that digital M&As significantly increase acquisition premiums. Evidence from patent-based identification points towards digital capabilities driving premium formation. Further analysis reveals that acquiring firms' management digital technology background strengthens the positive effect of digital M&As on premiums, while their digital transformation levels weaken this relationship. The effect is more pronounced in conglomerate acquisitions than in horizontal or vertical acquisitions. Additional tests show that digital M&A premiums reduce agency costs and enhance market value, particularly for firms with high absorption capacity, though they may crowd out future digital innovation. Our findings suggest that digital resource scarcity and expectations of synergistic value creation drive firms' willingness to pay premiums in digital acquisitions.

Title: Value (in)congruence of patent pledges and its impact on corporate green innovation
Authors: Jianyu Zhao, Jing Qu, Xixi Li, Xi Xi
Abstract: To provide firms with frontier solutions for fulfilling their social responsibilities, our study attempts to approach corporate green innovation from the novel angle of value (in)congruence of patent pledges. Patent pledges, as an important corporate financing source, entail a dual value portfolio comprising both technological and exclusionary values. However, seldom studies have examined how the dynamic (im)balance state between the two value forms of patent pledges drives firms' strategic actions such as green innovation. Using a longitudinal panel dataset that contains 86,961 patent records of 3011 Chinese manufacturing firms during 2012-2021, our findings reveal that the incongruence between technological and exclusionary values of patent pledges significantly promotes corporate green innovation, while the congruence between the two value forms appears to have no effect. Moreover, the external pressures arising from media reports and government regulations are identified as important contingencies while interpreting the significant impacts of value incongruence on green innovation. Our study tries to unravel how patent pledges foster firms' green innovation, and offers practical suggestions for firms’ strategic actions relating to green innovation.

Title: Bring time to the forefront: Sequence mode of ambidextrous innovation and its innovation performance
Authors: Jie Cen, Xiaofei Jing, Yan Yang, Jingxin Yan
Abstract: “Ambidexterity” has emerged as the mainstream paradigm in the field of innovation since the study by March (1991). Scholars have conducted extensive research on it, yielding fruitful results. However, despite being an essential dimension of “ambidexterity”, time has largely been viewed as a premise in the past research of ambidextrous innovation, meaning that the temporal mechanism in the process of ambidextrous innovation is still a black box. In this study, we introduce Optimal Matching Analysis (OMA), a technique originating from biology and adapted to social sciences that compares sequence similarity through operations (insertion/deletion/substitution) to map innovation trajectories, as a novel approach to innovation research, with the aim of elucidating on the varied sequence modes of ambidextrous innovation and exploring their innovation performance. Based on the patent and financial data of 538 listed companies in nine strategic emerging industries in China from 1986 to 2021, we reached the following conclusions: (1) The sequence modes of firms’ ambidextrous innovation can be divided into four types based on innovation level and innovation cooperation: exploration focus-cooperation swift mode, exploitation focus-cooperation increase mode, synchronization focus-low cooperation mode, and synchronization focus-cooperation decrease mode. (2) Different sequence modes demonstrate varying innovation performance. Firms in the exploration focus-cooperation swift mode achieve the highest innovation quantity; firms in the exploitation focus-cooperation increase mode attain high quantity but at the expense of quality; firms in the synchronization focus-low cooperation mode have the highest innovation quality; and firms in the synchronization focus-cooperation decrease mode have the lowest innovation performance. Propensity Score Matching (PSM) further validated the robustness of our findings by addressing potential endogeneity concerns. This study pioneers the integration of OMA into the realm of innovation to investigate the sequence mode of ambidextrous innovation. Furthermore, it employs a combination of OMA and regression analysis to examine the influence of diverse ambidextrous innovation sequence modes on firm-level innovation performance. This paper moves beyond the existing hypothesis of “synchronization” or “succession”, opening the black box of time in ambidextrous innovation research, promoting the further application of OMA in ambidextrous innovation, laying a foundation for subsequent sequence research.

Title: The empowerment mechanism of industrial digital platforms in the steel industry based on the dynamic capability view: A multiple-case study
Authors: Xiangfeng Chen, Chenyu Wang, Shenghao Xie, Shuting Li
Abstract: The rise of industrial digital platforms has accelerated the digital transformation of manufacturing industries. Existing research has examined the structure, value creation, and business models of industrial digital platforms; however, the intrinsic dynamics of platform evolution and the ways in which platform owners empower platform actors remain underexplored. Drawing on dynamic capability theory, this study employs a multi-case approach to explore the evolution and digital empowerment of industrial digital platforms within the steel industry. We identify five micro-foundational dynamic capabilities and three distinct empowerment pathways, revealing that the recursive relationship between platform evolution and empowerment shapes the development and competitiveness of industrial digital platforms. These findings offer a dynamic perspective on the evolutionary processes of industrial digital platforms, demonstrating how platform owners empower actors through informational, material, and financial flows. By highlighting the interplay between platform dynamic capabilities and empowerment mechanisms, this study offers valuable managerial insights for platform stakeholders aiming to navigate and optimize the digital transformation of traditional manufacturing industries.

Title: Co-creating a digital platform for smart working in healthcare: reconfiguring social exchange in internal digital transformation
Authors: Eduardo Pereira Seino, Lucas Miguel Alencar de Morais Correia, Alejandro G. Frank
Abstract: Digital technologies have profoundly transformed healthcare, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Healthcare 4.0. Among these technologies, digital platforms stand out as modular systems that evolve through collaborative and co-creative processes. However, limited attention has been given to how healthcare professionals participate in platform co-creation, how social exchange mechanisms sustain this process, and how tensions emerge from the coexistence of healthcare routines and digital transformation. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory (SET), we examine how trust, commitment, reciprocity, power, and sociotechnical tensions shape internal healthcare platform co-creation. We conducted a qualitative case study in a Brazilian teaching hospital that internalized the development of its primary information system and adopted a co-creative approach in which healthcare professionals assumed Product Owner roles for different platform modules. The empirical investigation combined 25 interviews, participant observation, and document analysis over seven months. The findings show that internal healthcare platform co-creation constitutes a distinct SET configuration in which trust depends on process visibility and responsiveness, reciprocity is associated with professional recognition and shared organizational outcomes, and power is shaped by internal hierarchies and asymmetries in technological expertise. Product Owners emerge as hybrid sociotechnical actors who mediate between healthcare work practices and technical development. Although co-creation enhances smart working by aligning digital solutions with professionals’ needs, it also generates persistent tensions related to technostress, cognitive overload, and competing attention demands between patient care and platform interaction. We argue that these tensions are inherent to healthcare digital transformation and must be continuously managed rather than eliminated.

Title: Inventor team diversity and patent quality: Gender–geography interaction and the role of national innovation system complexity
Authors: Daniel Coronado, Esther Ferrándiz, M. Rosario Marín, M. Carmen Puentes
Abstract: This paper examines how gender and geographic diversity in R&D teams, together with the complexity of national innovation systems (NISs), affect patent quality. While prior research has analyzed these aspects separately, we investigate their interactions and context-dependent effects. Using 32,043 patent families filed between 1991 and 2014 by leading aerospace and defense firms, we estimate several count models to assess the impact of team diversity and NIS complexity on patent quality. Results show that geographic diversity among inventors enhances patent quality, whereas gender diversity does not have a significant independent effect. Contrary to expectations, the interaction of gender and geographic diversity is negative and marginally significant, suggesting coordination challenges may outweigh complementarities. We also find partial evidence that NIS complexity enhances patent quality, though this effect is largely mediated by firm-specific characteristics. Finally, the benefits of geographically diverse collaborations are amplified in complex innovation systems, highlighting the role of robust institutional environments in leveraging spatial diversity in R&D teams.

Title: Exploring deglobalization effects on global innovation ecosystems, and the role of cosmo-localism
Authors: Ioanna Stylianou, Michael Christofi, Karolina Sallaku, Alfredo De Massis
Abstract: Over the past years profound changes in the public sentiment and policy environment suggest the beginning of a new era with reversal attitudes towards globalization. Deglobalization which is commonly defined as the process of decreasing interdependence among nations has recently become the focus of scholarly attention with particular interest on the deglobalization consequences. A significant question related with deglobalization is how innovation ecosystems adapt in such a new challenging environment. Within this context, the primary objective of this paper is to evaluate the role of deglobalization on the firm's eco-innovation performance directly and indirectly through its moderating effect on eco-innovation spillovers while considering the presence of cosmo-localism. Using a spatially-lagged X model (SLX) for a sample of 63 countries over the period 1990-2023 we shed light on the detrimental effects of deglobalization on eco-innovation performance, emphasizing at the same time the importance of cosmo-localism in terms of alleviating these consequences.

Title: Less is more: Leveraging bricolage and exaptation for frugal innovation and firm growth
Authors: Lianyong Xu, Zelong Wei, Yongchuan Bao
Abstract: How to deliver more value (functionality, sustainability) with limited resources and lower costs (affordability) presents firms with a paradox in developing frugal innovation. This study draws on the resource orchestration theory to investigate the effects of resource orchestration capabilities (i.e., bricolage and exaptation) on frugal innovation. Furthermore, we examined the moderating role of product modularization. We tested our hypotheses using data from 334 manufacturing firms (two managers in each firm) in China. Results show that both bricolage and exaptation foster frugal innovation, which in turn propels firm growth. Product modularization weakens the positive effect of bricolage on frugal innovation but does not strengthen the positive effect of exaptation on frugal innovation. The study contributes to the frugal innovation literature by exploring the mechanisms that drive frugal innovation from the perspective of resource orchestration.

Title: Profiling the Entrepreneurship and Innovation Ecosystem (EIE) of Crete: A Quintuple Innovation Helix perspective
Authors: Elias G. Carayannis, George Papamichail, Antonios Angelakis, Manolis Manioudis, Nikos - Rigert Zotas
Abstract: The article presents an in-depth analysis of the Entrepreneurship and Innovation Ecosystem (EIE) of Crete, employing the Quintuple Innovation Helix (QIH) framework to explore systemic capabilities and bottlenecks. Drawing on empirical data from 25 regional firms and key innovation actors, the study reveals a science-anchored yet structurally imbalanced ecosystem. While institutions -such as the University of Crete, the Foundation for Research and Technology-Hellas (FORTH) and the Science and Technology Park of Crete (STEP-C)- provide a robust academic base, commercialization pathways, innovation partnerships, and ecosystem coordination remain limited. The analysis uncovers gaps in venture funding, talent specialization, IP strategy, and civil society engagement. By mapping the maturity levels across the five helices—academia, industry, government, civil society, and the environment—the paper identifies strategic asymmetries and proposes two integrated prongs for ecosystem enhancement: structural functionality and firm-level resilience. A six-step roadmap for QIH implementation is outlined to guide regional innovation policy. The findings offer a replicable blueprint for other peripheral ecosystems seeking inclusive, knowledge-driven, and sustainability-aligned innovation growth.

Title: Artifacts as temporal operators: How digital artifact properties shape the develop-validate coupling in new venture creation
Authors: Kisito F. Nzembayie, André van Stel
Abstract: Why do some ventures appear to run on a faster clock than others? We argue that part of the answer lies in the artifacts from which ventures are built. Conceptualizing entrepreneurship as an artifact-mediated design process, we theorize digital artifact properties as temporal operators: they condition the coupling between development and validation and thereby shape the speed, sequencing, concurrency, and granularity of venture creation. Drawing on a longitudinal action design study informed by Action Design Research (ADR) principles, we examine a primary education technology (edtech) venture using time-stamped logs, telemetry, and digital artifacts across four design cycles and a subsequent observation phase. We show how modularity and its generative offspring—reprogrammability, traceability, and distributedness—are actualized through four sociotechnical mechanisms: flexible iteration, concurrent co-creation, decentralized co-creation, and data-driven operations. These mechanisms explain when development and validation overlap, when feedback cycles compress, and when sequential staging reappears. The study advances mechanism-based theorizing in digital entrepreneurship, adds a temporal dimension to entrepreneurship-as-design, and illustrates how ADR principles can support forward-oriented entrepreneurship process research.

Title: AI assimilation for sustainable and resilient supply chains: Role of green ambidexterity and cybersecurity awareness
Authors: Soumyadeb Chowdhury, Shuang Ren, Prasanta Kumar Dey
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely portrayed as a transformative enabler for sustainable and resilient supply chains; however, theory and empirical evidence remain fragmented regarding how AI-based capabilities are converted into sustainability performance outcomes and how these outcomes interact with supply chain resilience. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view, this study conceptualizes AI assimilation as a foundational dynamic capability and examines its role in shaping sustainable business performance and supply chain resilience through green ambidexterity innovation and cybersecurity awareness. Using a four-wave longitudinal survey of 199 UK-based supply chain managers, the study empirically tests a theoretical model employing partial least squares structural equation modelling technique. The findings show that AI assimilation is positively associated with sustainable business performance via green ambidexterity innovation, thereby opening the black box linking AI assimilation to sustainability outcomes. Cybersecurity awareness (CSA) emerged as a meta-capability that strengthened the effectiveness of AI assimilation on green ambidexterity innovation, extending CSA's role beyond risk mitigation to the strategic orchestration of AI-enabled green innovation. Additionally, the study reveals a sustainability–resilience paradox: sustainable business performance is negatively associated with supply chain resilience, challenging the prevailing assumption of their inherent complementarity. Theoretically, the study demonstrates how AI assimilation can generate sustainability benefits while simultaneously imposing resilience trade-offs. By integrating AI assimilation, green ambidexterity innovation, and cybersecurity awareness, the research offers a more nuanced understanding of the conditions under which embedding AI into business processes can foster sustainable but not necessarily resilient supply chain organizations.

Title: Unlocking the potential of digital entrepreneurship in turbulent times: A comprehensive overview
Authors: Kisito F. Nzembayie, Gustav Hägg, Agnieszka Kurczewska, Pierluigi Rippa, Magnus Klofsten, David Urbano
Abstract: Digital technologies are central to how entrepreneurs respond to external shocks and uncertainty, yet research about digital entrepreneurship lacks a conceptual architecture for theorising this relationship. This paper develops a multilevel framework for understanding digital entrepreneurship under conditions of turbulence and makes three contributions. First, we sharpen the distinction between digital entrepreneurship (DE) and entrepreneurship in the digital age (EDA), arguing that the ontological properties of digital artefacts create distinct opportunity structures requiring dedicated theorising. Second, we conceptualise turbulence not as a uniform exogenous shock but as a relational condition whose entrepreneurial consequences vary by level of analysis and by the type of digital mechanism through which actors respond. Third, we foreground a core paradox—the simultaneous democratising and exclusionary potential of digital technologies—and propose it as an organising tension for future research. The six papers in this collection anchor the framework across micro, meso, and macro levels and motivate a research agenda organised around four foundational questions.

Title: Evaluating creative work with artificial intelligence: Evidence from constrained innovation tasks
Authors: Valerio Fedele Addis, Giuseppe Attanasi, Giovanni Di Bartolomeo, Michele Mariella, Valentina Peruzzi
Abstract: We study whether a large language model can reliably evaluate human creativity in constrained, innovation-like tasks. Using expert-generated creative outputs from a validated experiment with workers in cultural and creative industries, we embed ChatGPT as an evaluator and benchmark its assessments against expert human judgments obtained through the Consensual Assessment Technique. Study 1 supports AI reliability by showing that AI-based creativity evaluations exhibit internal consistency comparable to that of expert judges across repeated and independent runs, even under conservative scenarios. Replacing a human judge with an AI evaluator does not reduce inter-rater reliability across drawing, mathematical, and verbal tasks. Beyond reliability, AI evaluations display three additional features that are difficult to achieve with human-only panels: lower evaluative variability, systematically higher scores consistent with a potentially more inclusive evaluative stance, and task-independence of evaluative standards. Study 2 further supports task-independence by showing that AI evaluations are structured along fluency, flexibility, originality, and elaboration, with dimension weights that adapt to task-specific constraints.

Title: More than just fair: Legitimizing AI through reciprocity, ethical AI characteristics and personal information sharing
Authors: Shahid Hussain, Asim Qazi, Violetta Wilk
Abstract: This research examines how perceived reciprocity and perceived ethical AI characteristics – fairness, accountability, and transparency (FAT principles) – shape consumers’ willingness to share personal information and its downstream consequences in AI-mediated consumer-brand interactions. Grounded in social exchange theory, we conceptualize personal information sharing as a behavioral gateway through which ethical exchange cues translate into perceived algorithmic legitimacy and intention to co-create value. Using a two-study design, consisting of a scenario-based experiment (n = 184) and a cross-sectional survey (n = 612), the findings of this research show that reciprocity and FAT principles robustly increase willingness to share personal information. Their effects on perceived algorithmic legitimacy and co-creation intentions operate primarily through information sharing rather than directly. Results further indicate that willingness to share personal information functions as a legitimacy-conferring act, supporting a bottom-up, interactional view of legitimacy formation in AI-mediated exchanges. By distinguishing information sharing-based participation from downstream value co-creation, this study advances a process-based account of engagement and offers actionable insights for designing ethically grounded AI systems that encourage voluntary data sharing and sustained consumer collaboration.

Title: Digital innovation ecosystem: a systematic mapping to understand how digital technologies are transforming innovation ecosystem
Abstract: Digital-enabled innovation ecosystems (DIEs) are currently experiencing a period of growth and are becoming increasingly important in addressing grand challenges, including sustainability, technological disruption and inclusive innovation. In this study, digital innovation ecosystems are interpreted as innovation ecosystems that are enabled by digital technologies, rather than as a distinct or separate ecosystem category. This study provides a thorough, theory-driven systematic literature review examining the adoption of digital technologies (DTs), including selected deep-tech innovation, to address these challenges within innovation ecosystems (IEs). Using descriptive, bibliographic, and content analysis methods, the review evaluates 581 scholarly articles, narrowing them down to 328 based on titles, keywords, and full-text analysis. This in-depth investigation reveals eight distinct thematic clusters representing thematic configurations of IEs that have been transformed through digital and deep-tech innovations and the evolution of the research field. These include: i) IE dynamics, evolution, and strategic interactions enabled by DTs; ii) Shaping IE through digital platform and data-driven collaboration; iii) Digital innovation and DTs for Entrepreneurial Ecosystem; iv) DTs for Knowledge Transfer and collaboration within Open IEs; v) DTs to promote sustainability within IEs; vi) DTs impact on University IE; vii) DTs for Industry 4.0 IEs; viii) DTs for Urban Innovation Ecosystems and Smart City development. We develop a holistic and multi-theoretical framework from these research thematic areas that captures the dynamic interplay between actors, technologies, institutional contexts and innovation processes, taking into account the context of grand challenges. This study contributes to mapping the evolution of IE under the digital era, and proposing a future research agenda that focuses on the transformative role of DIEs in addressing complex societal issues. This study contributes to the literature on IEs enabled by DTs and proposing their evolution into DIEs in addressing complex societal issues. A future resercah agenda is then proposed along with practical and policy implications.

Title: Seeking legitimacy and learning: an exploration of KTOs’ engagement with associations to improve knowledge exchange
Authors: Rosa Grimaldi, Azzurra Meoli, Andrea Piccaluga, Giovanni Tolin
Abstract: Knowledge Transfer Offices (KTOs) play a central role in enabling technology and knowledge sharing. While the literature has extensively explored their institutional and organizational characteristics, their engagement in associations that support knowledge exchange remains underexplored. These associations, which we define as Knowledge Exchange Associations (KEAs), are crucial actors that foster KTOs' development by providing access to resources, learning opportunities, and institutional visibility. Drawing on interorganizational relationship literature, this study investigates how KTOs' engagement with KEAs evolves over time, and which mechanisms drive such evolution. We present a longitudinal case study of Netval, the Italian KEA for research valorization, relying on multiple sources, including interviews, archival data, and direct observations. Our findings identify two main drivers of KTOs’ engagement in KEAs (i.e., building legitimacy and searching for learning) and show how they vary across three evolutionary phases of the KEA: aggregation, consolidation, and impact.

Title: Corrigendum to “Technology-enabled social innovations for enhancing emerging countries’ rural healthcare ecosystem: A grounded theory approach” [Technovation 154 (2026), 1-20, 103565]
Authors: Arti Barapatrey Jain, Bikramjit Ray Chaudhuri
Abstract: The authors regret the abstract and keywords are missing in the published article. ABSTRACT Our understanding of the role and relevance of technology in enabling social innovation (SI) for addressing grand challenges is limited. In most emerging countries, grand challenges—including but not limited to inequality, climate action, and access to essential public services such as healthcare and education—are characterised by systemic complexity, institutional barriers, and divergent stakeholder interdependencies. To address such grand challenges, these stakeholders must adopt both technologies and innovative approaches that are contextually relevant, scalable, and sustainable to create social value for the targeted beneficiaries. This study investigates the dynamics of technology-enabled SIs, facilitated by socially-oriented organisations, to address institutional voids in resource-constrained emerging countries, empirically grounded in India's rural healthcare context. Consequently, it examines the role of socially-oriented organisations in innovating, developing and/or implementing such initiatives using digital technologies. The theoretical framework, derived from primary data collected through qualitative inquiry and developed through the grounded theory, helps us visualise how technology-enabled SIs strengthen rural healthcare provision by leveraging digital technologies as key enablers. We derive an institutional-level ‘technology-enabled SI ecosystem’ framework, emerging through collaborative activities of socially-oriented organisations and the interlinking of technology-enabled SI initiatives, to co-create social value for rural beneficiaries and mitigate structural elements of institutional voids prevalent in emerging countries. This study makes three interconnected theoretical contributions to the field of technology and innovation management research. First, it theorises technology-enabled SI as a phenomenon distinct from traditional technology innovation, where digital technologies are fundamentally constitutive in creating social value. This distinction advances innovation management literature, as SI fundamentally prioritises social value co-creation to address grand challenges, unlike market-driven innovation which prioritises economic value creation. Second, it extends innovation ecosystem theory beyond economic value co-creation, to include social value co-creation. Finally, it advances institutional voids theory through technology-enabled SI initiatives in the emerging country context. Beyond the healthcare domain, our findings reveal the dynamics of technology-enabled SI in addressing grand challenges across various domains in resource-constrained contexts. Our research provides actionable insights for social innovators, emerging socially-oriented organisations, healthcare providers, funding agencies, and policymakers on harnessing technology-enabled SI initiatives to systematically address grand challenges in resource-constrained settings. KEYWORDS Technology-enabled social innovation; Socially-oriented organisations; Grand challenges; Institutional voids; Innovation ecosystem; Rural health; Indian rural healthcare ecosystem

Title: Business models as bottlenecks: How the absence of business models hampers desired technology transitions
Abstract: Research on technological transitions has long identified technology bottlenecks and strategic resource bottlenecks as impediments that could slow transitions. This paper adds another dimension and examines the undertheorized role of business models and how business model misalignments can constitute a third type of bottleneck. Based on a qualitative case study of electrification in the road transport industry, this paper explores the phenomenon of business model bottlenecks . The study shows that in contrast to technology bottlenecks and strategic resource bottlenecks, a business model bottleneck manifests itself as an unattractive void position. Resolving such a bottleneck requires adjustment of several interdependent business models, requiring actors to cooperate in new ways. The findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the interrelation between technology transitions and business model innovation.

Title: Innovation for grand challenges: the evolving role of service providers in Open Innovation ecosystems
Authors: Francesca Capella, Giovanni Tolin, Federico Frattini, Josip Kotlar
Abstract: Grand challenges such as climate change, resource scarcity, and public health pressures persist despite technological and economic progress, calling for collaborative, multi-actor approaches that leverage knowledge, technology, and innovation. Within this context, open innovation represents a key paradigm for fostering ecosystems that enable resource exchange and collaboration across organizational boundaries. While prior research has extensively examined the roles of large firms, SMEs, and public actors in this context, the evolving contributions of open innovation service providers in this field remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates how service providers are adapting to address grand challenges within open innovation ecosystems through qualitative empirical research. The study identifies nine collaborative practices and introduces a threefold framework, encompassing value creation, value capture, and value sharing processes, that helps in understanding their role. The results show that open innovation service providers are transitioning from facilitators to strategic orchestrators, enabling new forms of ecosystem resilience and collective impact. This work advances theoretical understanding and offers practical insights into how more inclusive, adaptive, and impact-oriented open innovation ecosystems can be mobilized to address grand challenges. • The study advances value management theory in open innovation (OI) by introducing value sharing as a distinct and complementary dimension to value creation and value capture, offering a richer understanding of collaborative dynamics in grand challenge–oriented innovation ecosystems. • By systematically mapping open innovation service providers and their practices, the study positions them as central ecosystem actors that move beyond facilitation toward strategic orchestration of Open Innovation initiatives. • The analysis show how service providers contribute across value creation, value capture, and value sharing processes, highlighting their critical role in enabling collective action and ecosystem resilience when addressing grand societal challenges. • The paper develops a structured framework that categorizes service providers' roles and practices, providing actionable guidance for senior managers and policymakers to align open innovation initiatives with organizational strategies while addressing grand challenges.

Title: From infrastructure to innovation: How integrated PLM systems enable digital twin and thread capabilities in business-to-business manufacturing
Abstract: Industrial manufacturers invest heavily in Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) systems, digital twins, and digital threads, yet many of these efforts remain fragmented, yielding uneven innovation outcomes. A critical gap exists regarding how these technologies interrelate within digital infrastructure and the conditions under which they enable different forms of digital innovation in Business-to-Business (B2B) manufacturing contexts. This study examines how integrated PLM (iPLM) infrastructure enables digital-twin and thread capabilities, and how those capabilities drive innovation in processes, products, and servitization. We reconceptualize digital twins and threads as emergent functionalities of mature iPLM infrastructure and extend dynamic capabilities theory to digital infrastructure contexts using a sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring framework. Through a qualitative multiple-case study of four asset-heavy manufacturers, involving 25 executive interviews, archival analysis, and the Gioia methodology, we develop a process model of the infrastructure-to-innovation pathway. Infrastructure maturity functions as the enabling condition through three recurring features: disciplined product definition and change control, stable cross-system integration, and consistent data governance. Three differentiated innovation pathways emerge. Digital process innovation is driven by sensing capabilities that detect and diagnose operational signals. Digital product innovation emerges when sensing and seizing work together, strengthened by digital twin functionality that enables simulation-based learning and virtual validation. Digital servitization emerges from reconfiguring capabilities, with digital thread functionality providing end-to-end lifecycle traceability during business model transitions. This research contributes to digital innovation theory by theorizing iPLM as a generative infrastructure whose maturity shapes the forms of innovation that are achievable, and by offering manufacturers actionable guidance on sequencing digital investments toward specific innovation objectives.

Title: Too much of a good thing? Venture capital chase and firm innovation
Authors: Yiyuan Mai, Xinyi Cheng, Jun Li, Zhuxin Ye, Yuping Wu
Abstract: Venture capital (VC) is a vital source of financing for firms to support their growth and innovation. In China, however, VC tends to concentrate disproportionately and repeatedly on a few high-profile firms, through multiple rounds, large funding amounts, and many participating investors. The impact of this intense VC chase, especially on firm innovation, has received little attention in the existing literature. Based on data of companies listed on the Growth Enterprise Market from 2010 to 2024, with observation windows spanning three years before and after each firm's IPO, this study explores the relationship between VC chase and innovation performance of invested firms. The empirical results reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship: while a moderate level of VC chase is positively associated with firm innovation, excessive chase is negatively associated with it. Furthermore, this study analyzes the boundary conditions of this relationship and finds that the inverted U-shaped relationship is more pronounced in firms with lower R&D intensity or greater technological distance from industry leaders. This study enriches the understanding of how VC influences firm innovation by conceptualizing VC chase as a dynamic, multidimensional pattern of investment and interpreting its effects through a temporal pacing and innovation rhythm perspective, and provides theoretical insights for policymakers and investment institutions to establish a well-developed capital market and efficient investment mechanisms.

Title: Identification of driving factors in national innovation ecosystems under the PSR framework: Based on machine learning algorithms
Authors: Neng Shen, Lianjun Wu, Jing Zhang, Lin Zhang
Abstract: To address the challenge of insufficient momentum for sustainable global innovation development, a growing number of countries are elevating the cultivation of innovation ecosystems to the level of national strategy, aiming to secure discourse power and initiative in future international competition. Previously, studies have primarily focused on the conceptualization and evolutionary mechanisms of National Innovation Ecosystems (NIEs), and have extended the indicator systems of National Innovation Systems to evaluate NIEs performance. However, there remains a notable gap in applying ecological theories to construct NIEs indicator systems, as well as a lack of exploration into the driving effects of national macro-level characteristics on NIEs. Addressing this research gap, this study draws upon the food chain perspective and the quadruple helix model to propose a novel conceptual framework for understanding the interactions among actors within the NIEs. Furthermore, we introduce the Pressure-State-Response (PSR) framework to establish a system of driving factors centered on National Risk, National Openness, and National Governance. This research provides a systematic analytical tool for clarifying the interactive logic among multi-level innovation actors.
